items.html: Optic neuritis epidemiology. About 75 percent of cases occur in women, in patients aged 18 to 45.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 23

src.question: A 27-year-old patient is diagnosed with optic neuritis. What proportion of cases occur in women?
src.explanation: in patients aged 18 to 45.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Inflammatory markers in arteritic optic neuropathy. They help rule the diagnosis in or out; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are markedly raised.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 51

src.question: A 76-year-old woman is being assessed for arteritic optic neuropathy. What role do the inflammatory markers play?
src.key: They help rule the diagnosis in or out
src.explanation: Correct; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are markedly raised.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Arteritic optic neuropathy outlook. The outlook depends on the duration of symptoms and when steroids began, which is why early therapy is critical.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 51

src.question: An 80-year-old woman is treated for arteritic optic neuropathy. What does the outlook depend on?
src.key: Duration of symptoms and when steroids began
src.explanation: which is why early therapy is critical.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Secondary angle-closure glaucoma. Drainage can be obstructed by tumor, scarring or other mechanical causes.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 14

src.question: A 61-year-old woman has secondary angle-closure glaucoma. What can obstruct the drainage in this form?
src.key: Tumor, scarring or other mechanical causes

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Central retinal artery occlusion and general health. Stroke risk is markedly increased, since plaque reaching the retinal artery implies more in the carotids.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 37

src.question: A 68-year-old man with a central retinal artery occlusion asks about his general health risk. What should he be told?
src.key: His stroke risk is markedly increased
src.explanation: Correct; plaque reaching the retinal artery implies more in the carotids.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Branch versus central retinal vein occlusion. In a branch occlusion a smaller branch vein is blocked, so only part of the retina is affected, unlike central retinal vein occlusion.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 35

src.question: A 62-year-old man has painless loss of only the lower half of the vision in one eye, with hemorrhages confined to the upper retina. How does this differ from a central retinal vein occlusion?
src.key: A smaller branch vein is blocked
src.explanation: so only part of the retina is affected.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Anticholinergics in angle closure. Systemic anticholinergic medications such as atropine are a risk factor for acute angle closure, in which the iris blocks the drainage circuit and pressure rises, so they can worsen angle-closure glaucoma.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 14

src.question: A 63-year-old man with angle-closure glaucoma is about to start a medication for overactive bladder. Which counseling point applies?
src.key: Anticholinergic drugs can worsen his glaucoma
src.explanation: Correct — systemic anticholinergic medications such as atropine are a risk factor for acute angle closure, in which the iris blocks the drainage circuit and pressure rises.

items.html: Amaurosis fugax source. Painless monocular blackouts lasting under a minute most likely arise from a carotid or cardiac embolus, most commonly a transient ischemic attack of retinal origin.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 5

src.question: A 71-year-old woman has had three episodes of painless monocular blackout, each lasting under a minute. What is the most likely source?
src.explanation: Most commonly a transient ischemic attack of retinal origin.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Antihypertensive timing in non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. The antihypertensive dose may be moved away from bedtime to avoid nocturnal hypotension, which can worsen the condition.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 52

src.question: A 57-year-old man with non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy takes an antihypertensive at bedtime. Which change may be considered?
src.key: Moving the dose away from bedtime
src.explanation: to avoid nocturnal hypotension, which can worsen the condition.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Optic disc in anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Sudden painless vision loss with a swollen, pale disc and loss of side or central vision is the expected picture.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: A 68-year-old woman has sudden painless vision loss. What optic disc appearance is expected in anterior ischemic optic neuropathy?
src.explanation: with loss of side or central vision.

items.section_title: 3.9 · Care strategies — adult and elderly Objective b
items.html: Sudden painless monocular vision loss. Urgent ophthalmology involvement is the non-negotiable step, because each of these diagnoses is sight-threatening and time-dependent.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: A 69-year-old man has sudden painless monocular vision loss and no other findings. Which single step is treated as non-negotiable?
src.explanation: Correct; each of these diagnoses is sight-threatening and time-dependent.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. With markedly raised inflammatory markers, treatment starts with intravenous methylprednisolone for three days, then a slow oral taper; early therapy is critical.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 51

src.question: A 78-year-old woman has arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Her inflammatory markers are markedly raised. What is done first?
src.explanation: three days, then a slow oral taper; early therapy is critical.

items.html: Why screen for open-angle glaucoma. It is asymptomatic at onset, and the damage it does cannot be reversed.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: A 62-year-old man asks why his eyes are screened when nothing hurts. Why is open-angle glaucoma screened for?
src.explanation: and the damage it does cannot be reversed.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Iris lesion size concerning for melanoma. A lesion over 3 mm across and over 1 mm deep raises concern for melanoma; a nevus is usually smaller and flat.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 45

src.question: A 63-year-old man has an iris lesion. Which dimensions raise concern for melanoma?
src.key: Over 3 mm across and over 1 mm deep
src.explanation: A nevus is usually smaller and flat.

items.html: Optic nerve pallor without cupping. This favors ocular ischemic syndrome, which is underlain by carotid stenosis.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: A patient has optic nerve pallor rather than cupping. Which diagnosis does that favor?
src.explanation: and carotid stenosis underlies it.

items.html: Dry versus wet macular degeneration. About 80 percent of macular degeneration is the dry form, leaving roughly 20 percent wet.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 11

src.question: An 82-year-old man is told he has the dry form. What share of macular degeneration is dry?
src.explanation: leaving roughly 20 percent wet.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Uveal melanoma outlook by site. Iris melanoma carries a better outlook than ciliary body melanoma, with roughly 4 to 10 percent mortality for the iris against far worse for the ciliary body.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: Two patients have uveal melanoma, one of the iris and one of the ciliary body. What do you expect?
src.key: The iris tumor carries the better outlook
src.explanation: roughly 4 to 10 percent mortality against far worse.

items.html: Eye care in diabetes. Annual ophthalmology review should be arranged, because a medical eye risk needs the medical specialist.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: A 58-year-old woman with diabetes has never had an eye examination. What do you arrange?
src.explanation: A medical eye risk needs the medical specialist.

items.section_title: 4.11 · The differentials — what else looks like this
items.html: Small flat pigmented iris spot. A flat, 2 mm, avascular pigmented iris spot is likely benign but should be referred to ophthalmology to document and monitor, as a baseline is needed.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 49

src.question: A 35-year-old man has a flat, 2 mm, avascular pigmented iris spot noticed at a routine visit. What do you do?
src.key: Refer to ophthalmology to document and monitor
src.explanation: Likely benign, but a baseline is needed.

items.html: Why open-angle glaucoma goes unnoticed. It is painless and spares central vision early, which is why screening exists.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: A 72-year-old man asks why he lost side vision without noticing. Why does open-angle glaucoma go unnoticed?
src.key: It is painless and spares central vision early
src.explanation: which is why screening exists.

items.html: Timing of cataract surgery. Surgery can be deferred until the cataract affects daily life, unless another eye disease forces the issue.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 39

src.question: A 71-year-old man has a cataract but manages daily life without difficulty. What do you advise?
src.key: Defer until it affects daily life
src.explanation: unless another eye disease forces the issue.

items.html: Double vision that resolves when either eye is covered. Binocular diplopia means misalignment until proven otherwise, so the next step is to assess ocular alignment and cranial nerves.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 25

src.question: A 50-year-old woman develops horizontal double vision that resolves when either eye is covered. What is the next step?
src.key: Assess ocular alignment and cranial nerves
src.explanation: Binocular diplopia means misalignment until proven otherwise.

items.html: Cataract referral urgency. A cataract with uveitis in the same eye needs urgent referral, whereas an isolated cataract is a routine referral.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: A 62-year-old woman has a cataract and uveitis in the same eye. How urgent is referral?
src.explanation: An isolated cataract is a routine referral.

items.html: Delayed appointment for suspected retinoblastoma. Call the specialist and get the appointment brought forward, and document the request if they will not.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: You suspect retinoblastoma in a 2-year-old and the offered appointment is in two months. What do you do?
src.key: Call the specialist and get it brought forward
src.explanation: and document it if they will not.

items.html: Long eyeball. A long eyeball predicts blurred distance vision with clear near vision, because myopia focuses distant objects in front of the retina.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: A 19-year-old woman is told her eyeball is long. What does that predict about her vision?
src.explanation: Myopia focuses distant objects in front of the retina.

items.html: Glaucoma drops. Drops protect the vision that remains, because damage already done cannot be reversed.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: A 74-year-old man with glaucoma asks why he must keep using drops when he sees no better. What do you say?
src.key: They protect the vision he still has
src.explanation: Damage already done cannot be reversed.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Growing vascular iris lesion. A raised pigmented iris lesion with a feeder vessel that has grown raises real concern and warrants referral to ophthalmology, likely ocular oncology.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: A 60-year-old woman has a raised pigmented iris lesion with a feeder vessel that has grown. What is the next step?
src.key: Refer to ophthalmology, likely ocular oncology
src.explanation: Growth and vascularity raise real concern.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Ciliary body versus iris melanoma. Ciliary body melanoma does worse because it is hidden and found later, whereas an iris lesion is visible and caught earlier.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: A 66-year-old man asks why melanoma of the ciliary body does worse than melanoma of the iris. Why?
src.key: It is hidden, so it is found later
src.explanation: An iris lesion is visible and caught earlier.

items.html: Recovery after cataract surgery. Recovery is prompt and near-complete in almost all isolated cases, with complications infrequent overall.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 39

src.question: A 73-year-old woman asks what recovery after cataract surgery is like. What do you tell her?
src.key: Prompt and near-complete in almost all isolated cases
src.explanation: with complications infrequent overall.

items.html: Amblyopia outcome with patching. Outcome is good, though vision is not always fully normal, and starting treatment before age five is better still.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: A 6-year-old boy starts patching for amblyopia. What do you tell his parents about outcome?
src.key: Good, though not always fully normal vision
src.explanation: and starting before five is better still.

items.html: Sharp worsening of central blur in dry macular degeneration. A rapid change over a week raises concern for conversion to the wet form, in which new vessels bleed.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 14

src.question: A 79-year-old man with known dry macular degeneration reports his central blur worsened sharply over a week. What is the concern?
src.explanation: New vessels bleeding cause a rapid change.

items.section_title: 4.11 · The differentials — what else looks like this
items.html: Enlarging pigmented conjunctival lesion. Refer to ophthalmology for assessment, because growth in a pigmented lesion demands specialist review.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 53

src.question: A 66-year-old man has an enlarging pigmented conjunctival lesion. What is the next step?
src.explanation: Growth in a pigmented lesion demands specialist review.

items.html: Third nerve palsy with pupil involvement. Sudden ptosis, a dilated pupil and an eye deviated down and out require urgent exclusion of an aneurysm compressing the third nerve; pupil involvement makes this an emergency.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: A 62-year-old man has sudden ptosis, a dilated pupil and an eye deviated down and out. What must be excluded urgently?
src.key: An aneurysm compressing the third nerve
src.explanation: Pupil involvement makes this an emergency.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Stable iris nevus. The risk of transformation to cancer is low, but surveillance continues because the risk is not zero.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 49

src.question: A 40-year-old woman with a stable iris nevus asks whether it will become cancer. What do you tell her?
src.key: The risk of transformation is low
src.explanation: but surveillance continues because it is not zero.

items.html: Objection to covering one eye. A toddler who cries only when the right eye is covered sees poorly with the left eye, because he objects when his good eye is taken away.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 32

src.question: A toddler cries only when his right eye is covered. What does the examiner conclude?
src.explanation: He objects when his good eye is taken away.

items.html: Improved near vision with nuclear cataract. The lens shifts toward myopia, so suddenly reading without glasses is explained, because nuclear change blurs distance more than near.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 37

src.question: A 69-year-old man with a nuclear cataract finds he can suddenly read without glasses. Why?
src.key: The lens has shifted him myopic
src.explanation: Nuclear change blurs distance more than near.

items.html: Pterygium surgery. Refer for surgical excision when a pterygium grows onto the cornea and distorts vision.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 28

src.question: A 47-year-old surfer has a pterygium that has advanced 2 mm onto the cornea over two years and now induces astigmatism. What is the appropriate management?
src.explanation: Surgery is indicated when it grows onto the cornea and distorts vision.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Sudden painless monocular vision loss. Immediate ophthalmology referral is the next step; it is a stroke of the eye, and the window is measured in minutes to hours.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 40

src.question: A 68-year-old man presents 40 minutes after sudden painless monocular vision loss. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: It is a stroke of the eye — the window is measured in minutes to hours.

items.html: Recurrent anterior uveitis with inflammatory back pain. Back pain that improves with exercise and worsens with rest points to HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathy, the ankylosing spondylitis association, which is why the systemic history matters.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 62

src.question: A 34-year-old man with recurrent anterior uveitis is being investigated. His back pain improves with exercise and worsens with rest. Which association is most likely?
src.explanation: Correct — the ankylosing spondylitis association, which is why the systemic history matters.

items.html: Absent red reflex in an infant. It demands urgent ophthalmology referral, because cataract and retinoblastoma both present this way.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 38

src.question: A 5-week-old infant is found to have an absent red reflex in the left eye at the newborn check. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: An absent red reflex demands urgent assessment — cataract and retinoblastoma both present this way.

items.html: Escalation for red, crusted lid margins. Lid hygiene comes first; if there is no improvement after two weeks, add a topical antibiotic, then oral antibiotics.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 19

src.question: A 47-year-old woman with red, crusted lid margins and a frothy tear film has used lid hygiene twice daily for two weeks with no improvement. What is the next step?
src.explanation: Lid hygiene first; no better after two weeks, escalate to topical, then oral antibiotics.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Branch versus central retinal vein occlusion. In the branch form the clot is in a branch vein, so hemorrhage is confined to that territory and only part of the retina is affected.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 35

src.question: How does branch retinal vein occlusion differ from the central form?
src.key: The clot is in a branch vein
src.explanation: Correct — hemorrhage is confined to that territory. Only part of the retina is affected.

items.html: Occlusion objection test. A child who objects when one eye is covered has amblyopia in the other eye, because the child objects when the good eye is covered.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 32

src.question: A 3-year-old boy is unbothered when his left eye is covered, but becomes fussy when his right eye is covered. What does this test show?
src.explanation: The occlusion objection test: the child objects when the GOOD eye is covered.

items.html: Scleritis workup. Severe deep eye pain that wakes from sleep, with a bluish hue to the sclera, warrants an autoimmune workup, because scleritis is frequently associated with systemic autoimmune disease, including connective tissue disease.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 50

src.question: A 49-year-old woman has severe deep eye pain that wakes her at night, with a bluish hue to the sclera visible in daylight. What systemic evaluation is warranted?
src.explanation: Correct — scleritis is frequently associated with systemic autoimmune disease. For connective tissue disease.

items.html: Age and amblyopia treatment. Treatment works less well as maturity approaches; the earlier amblyopia is treated, the better the outcome.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 33

src.question: A 10-year-old boy is diagnosed with amblyopia for the first time. Why does his age matter?
src.key: Treatment works less well as maturity approaches
src.explanation: Correct — the earlier it is treated, the better the outcome.

items.html: Causes of ectropion. Aging, scarring and congenital causes can produce ectropion, and seventh nerve palsy causes ectropion only.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 12

src.question: Which of these can cause ectropion?
src.explanation: Correct — and seventh nerve palsy causes ectropion ONLY. Congenital causes also produce ectropion.

items.html: Contact lens corneal ulcer. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the organism of greatest concern with contact lens wear, and it can perforate the cornea rapidly.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 60

src.question: A 22-year-old woman who sleeps in her contact lenses has a painful red right eye with a white spot on the cornea and an overlying epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein. Which organism is of greatest concern?
src.explanation: The contact lens association makes this the organism to fear, and it can perforate rapidly.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Lid margin laceration. A laceration through the lid margin needs specialist repair with meticulous approximation, because a poor repair leaves a permanent notch and chronic irritation.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 27

src.question: A 29-year-old woman has a lid laceration through the lid MARGIN of the upper lid. Why does that require specialist repair?
src.key: A poor repair leaves a permanent notch
src.explanation: Correct — margin-involving lacerations need meticulous approximation. And chronic irritation.

items.html: Suspected globe rupture. Immediate management is a rigid shield, nil by mouth, antiemetics and urgent referral; avoid anything that raises intraocular pressure and apply no pressure to the eye.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 17

src.question: A 39-year-old woman has a suspected globe rupture. What is the immediate management?
src.key: Rigid shield, nil by mouth, antiemetics, urgent referral
src.explanation: Nothing that raises intraocular pressure, and no pressure on the eye.

items.html: Cycloplegic in anterior uveitis. It relieves pain and prevents synechiae by resting the ciliary body and keeping the iris from adhering to the lens.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 63

src.question: A 38-year-old man with anterior uveitis is prescribed a cycloplegic alongside the steroid. What is its purpose?
src.key: To relieve pain and prevent synechiae
src.explanation: Correct — it rests the ciliary body and keeps the iris from adhering to the lens.

items.html: Posterior vitreous detachment without a retinal break. Advise return if a curtain or shadow appears; that warning converts this from observation to emergency.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 27

src.question: A 55-year-old man reports flashes and floaters but no field loss. Examination shows a posterior vitreous detachment with no retinal break. What is the appropriate advice?
src.key: Return if a curtain or shadow appears
src.explanation: Correct — the warning is what converts this from observation to emergency.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Intraocular pressure in glaucoma. Pressure may be either normal or elevated in this disease.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 18

src.question: A 61-year-old woman is being assessed for glaucoma. What can the intraocular pressure be?
src.explanation: Correct — pressure may be normal OR raised in this disease.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Non-arteritic share of anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. The non-arteritic form accounts for ninety to ninety-five percent of cases and is by far the commoner form.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 48

src.question: What proportion of anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is the non-arteritic form?
src.explanation: Correct — it is by far the commoner form.

items.html: Imaging in dacryoadenitis. Contrast computed tomography of the orbits and paranasal sinuses is used when indicated, not automatically on presentation.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 23

src.question: A 29-year-old woman has dacryoadenitis. Which statement about imaging is correct?
src.explanation: Contrast computed tomography of the orbits and paranasal sinuses is used when indicated, not automatically on presentation.

items.html: Corneal ulcer with intraocular inflammation. A hypopyon, layered white cells in the anterior chamber, indicates significant intraocular inflammation.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 61

src.question: A 26-year-old man has a corneal ulcer. Which examination finding indicates significant intraocular inflammation?
src.explanation: Correct — layered white cells in the anterior chamber.

items.html: Holding text further away with unchanged distance vision. The lens stiffens, so accommodation fails.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 18

src.question: A 46-year-old man finds he must hold text further away to read it, while distance vision is unchanged. What is the mechanism?
src.key: The lens stiffens, so accommodation fails
src.explanation: Correct — the A in PERRLA is what is failing.

items.html: Vesicular rash on forehead and nose tip. The ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve is involved, and involvement of the nose tip signals ocular involvement.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 57

src.question: A 68-year-old woman has a vesicular rash over her right forehead and the tip of her nose, with a red painful eye. Which cranial nerve division is involved?
src.key: The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
src.explanation: Correct — V1 of cranial nerve V. Involvement of the nose tip signals ocular involvement.

items.html: Hutchinson sign. Vesicles on the tip of the nose indicate a high likelihood of ocular involvement, because the nasociliary branch supplies both the nose tip and the globe.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 57

src.question: A 71-year-old man has a painful vesicular rash in a band across his right forehead, sparing the midline, with vesicles on the tip of his nose. What does the nasal tip involvement indicate?
src.key: A high likelihood of ocular involvement
src.explanation: Correct — Hutchinson sign; the nasociliary branch supplies both the nose tip and the globe.

items.html: Posterior uveitis. It involves the choroid and/or the retina, that is, choroiditis and retinitis.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 64

src.question: Which structures does POSTERIOR uveitis involve?
src.explanation: Correct — choroiditis and retinitis.

items.html: Course of viral conjunctivitis. It worsens for about a week, then clears, with resolution taking two to three weeks, and it is highly contagious throughout.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 37

src.question: A 30-year-old man with viral conjunctivitis says his eye looked worse on day five than on day two and asks whether the treatment has failed. What should he be told?
src.key: It worsens for a week, then clears
src.explanation: and it is highly contagious throughout. Resolution takes two to three weeks.

items.html: Viral conjunctivitis education. Strict hand hygiene is the key advice, as the condition is highly contagious; contagious precautions are the central education point.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 37

src.question: A 32-year-old teacher with viral conjunctivitis asks what she should do about work. What is the key advice?
src.key: Strict hand hygiene, as it is highly contagious
src.explanation: Correct — contagious precautions are the central education point.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Enlarging vascular conjunctival lesion. A raised pigmented conjunctival lesion that has enlarged and has its own feeding vessels needs urgent referral for biopsy, since growth and intrinsic vascularity are the concerning features.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 53

src.question: A 67-year-old woman has a raised pigmented conjunctival lesion that has enlarged over six months and has its own feeding vessels. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Growth and intrinsic vascularity are the concerning features.

items.html: Acquired nystagmus in an adult. It suggests an underlying neurological cause; it is not benign and requires investigation.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 5

src.question: A 45-year-old woman has acquired nystagmus with oscillopsia. What does the acquired onset suggest?
src.explanation: Correct — acquired nystagmus in an adult is not benign. It requires investigation.

items.html: Hyphema instructions. Strenuous activity and bending must be avoided, as both raise the risk of rebleeding.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 25

src.question: A 20-year-old man with a hyphema is given instructions for the next five days. Which activity must he avoid?
src.explanation: Correct — both raise the risk of rebleeding.

items.html: Infectious cause of posterior uveitis. Toxoplasma gondii causes chorioretinitis and is a classic infectious cause of posterior uveitis.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 65

src.question: A 38-year-old man with posterior uveitis is being investigated for an infectious cause. Which organism causes chorioretinitis?
src.explanation: Correct — a classic infectious cause of posterior uveitis.

items.section_title: 4.11 · The differentials — what else looks like this
items.html: Iris nevus follow-up. Surveillance with dilated review is more frequent at first, then annual; the early checks confirm the nevus is not growing.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 49

src.question: How is an iris nevus followed up?
src.key: More often at first, then annually
src.explanation: Correct — surveillance with dilated review. The early checks confirm it is not growing.

items.html: Corneal abrasion follow-up. Periodic re-examination is required, alongside a topical broad-spectrum antibacterial, to confirm healing and exclude infection.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 18

src.question: Which follow-up does a corneal abrasion require?
src.explanation: alongside a topical broad-spectrum antibacterial. To confirm healing and exclude infection.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Care strategies, adult and elderly Objective h
items.html: Tonic pupil in an otherwise well person. Management is reassurance once causes are excluded; it is benign, though the anisocoria may persist.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 37

src.question: A 31-year-old woman with a tonic pupil is otherwise well. What is the management?
src.explanation: Correct — it is benign, though the anisocoria may persist.

items.html: Fellow eye in acute angle closure. The other eye receives prophylactic iridotomy, because it shares the crowded anatomy and is anatomically at risk.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 20

src.question: A 63-year-old man is treated for acute angle-closure in one eye. What is done about the other eye?
src.explanation: Correct — the fellow eye shares the crowded anatomy. The fellow eye is anatomically at risk.

items.html: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with deeper involvement. If there is retinitis, choroiditis or optic neuritis, treatment is steroids and intravenous acyclovir.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 59

src.question: A 70-year-old woman has herpes zoster ophthalmicus with keratitis. Which treatment is indicated if there is retinitis, choroiditis or optic neuritis?

items.html: Mild pre-septal cellulitis. In a systemically well child with reliable follow-up, manage with oral antibiotics and early review at 24 to 48 hours.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 53

src.question: A 4-year-old girl has pre-septal cellulitis. She is systemically well and her parents are reliable. What is the appropriate management?
src.explanation: Correct for mild pre-septal disease in a well child with reliable follow-up. Review at 24 to 48 hours.

items.section_title: 1.1 · The red eye, before you name a diagnosis
items.html: Chemical eye injury. This is emergent: copious irrigation starts at once, before visual acuity, imaging or referral calls.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 3

src.question: A 28-year-old worker has a chemical splash to the eye. What is the single most important action?
src.explanation: Chemical injury is emergent: copious irrigation starts at once, before visual acuity, imaging or referral calls.

items.html: Stakes of untreated idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Permanent vision loss from optic nerve damage is the risk; the vision, not the headache, drives treatment.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 5

src.question: A 27-year-old woman with idiopathic intracranial hypertension asks what is at stake if it is not treated. What should she be told?
src.key: Permanent loss from optic nerve damage
src.explanation: Correct — the vision, not the headache, is what drives treatment.

items.html: Optic neuritis course. Vision usually recovers substantially over weeks, though color desaturation may persist.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 24

src.question: A 32-year-old woman with optic neuritis asks about her vision. What is the expected course?
src.key: Vision usually recovers substantially over weeks
src.explanation: though color desaturation may persist.

items.html: Yellowish raised nasal conjunctival nodule not reaching the cornea. Sun, dust and wind protection with lubricating drops controls symptoms but will not resolve the nodule.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 28

src.question: A 39-year-old landscaper has a yellowish raised nodule on the nasal conjunctiva at the 3 o'clock position of the left eye. It does not reach the cornea. He asks whether treatment will make it go away. What should he be told?
src.key: It controls symptoms but will not resolve it
src.explanation: Sun, dust and wind protection with lubricating drops.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Horner syndrome. A droopy lid, small pupil that reacts to light and dry face (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) in a smoker with a months-long cough means an apical lung tumor, a Pancoast tumor, must be excluded.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 28

src.question: A 57-year-old smoker has a droopy right upper lid and a small right pupil that reacts to light. The right side of his face is dry. He has had a cough for three months. Which statement about his diagnosis is correct?
src.key: Horner syndrome, and an apical lung tumor must be excluded
src.explanation: Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis; a Pancoast tumor is the concern with this history.

items.html: Preauricular node in conjunctivitis. Bacterial conjunctivitis otherwise lacks a node, so severe purulent discharge with a node points to gonococcal disease.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 41

src.question: A 23-year-old man has severe purulent conjunctivitis with a palpable preauricular node. Why is the node significant here?
src.key: Bacterial conjunctivitis otherwise lacks a node
src.explanation: Severe purulent discharge WITH a node points to gonococcal disease.

items.html: Uncomplicated corneal abrasion. A well-defined epithelial defect with no infiltrate is treated with topical antibiotic ointment and analgesia, with follow-up to confirm healing.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 18

src.question: A 26-year-old woman has severe pain, tearing and photophobia in the right eye after a fingernail scratch. Fluorescein shows a well-defined epithelial defect with no infiltrate. What is the most appropriate treatment?
src.explanation: with follow-up to confirm healing.

items.html: Amsler grid. It is a self-monitoring tool to detect distortion or a missing area, which suggests conversion of dry macular degeneration to the wet form.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 14

src.question: A 72-year-old woman with dry macular degeneration is given a grid of straight lines to check at home. What is she being asked to detect?
src.explanation: Correct — the Amsler grid is a self-monitoring tool for exactly that change. That suggests conversion to the wet form.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Stable flat pigmented iris lesion. A lesion unchanged on photographs over five years, with no pupil distortion, is managed with photographic monitoring, as documented stability supports a benign nevus.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 48

src.question: A 46-year-old man has a flat, pigmented iris lesion that has been unchanged on photographs over five years, with no distortion of the pupil. What is the most appropriate management?
src.explanation: Documented stability over years supports a benign nevus.

items.html: Entropion and the cornea. The key question with entropion is always whether the lashes have damaged the cornea, assessed by slit lamp examination; an epithelial defect from lash contact means the cornea is now involved.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 13
CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 13

src.question: A 76-year-old man with entropion has developed a corneal epithelial defect from lash contact. What does this change?
src.explanation: Correct — the slit lamp question in these lid malpositions is always whether the cornea has been affected. Which is what the examination looks for.

also.key: Slit lamp examination to assess whether the cornea has been involved
also.explanation: Correct — the question with entropion is always whether the lashes have damaged the cornea.

items.html: Manifest misalignment in a child. An eye that turns inward, with the other eye moving to take up fixation on the cover test, needs referral to ophthalmology to prevent amblyopia.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 29

src.question: A 3-year-old boy has an eye that turns inward. The cover test shows the left eye moving out to take up fixation when the right is covered. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Manifest misalignment in a child needs assessment to prevent amblyopia.

items.html: Neonatal purulent conjunctivitis timing. Onset on day 2 of life suggests Neisseria gonorrhoeae, since gonococcal disease presents in the first few days while chlamydial disease presents later, around days 5 to 14.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 44

src.question: A newborn develops a purulent conjunctivitis on day 2 of life. Which organism is most likely, given the timing?
src.explanation: Gonococcal disease presents in the first few days; chlamydial disease presents later, around days 5 to 14.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Suspected arteritic vision loss. Sudden painless vision loss with scalp tenderness, jaw aching on chewing and a markedly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate calls for high-dose corticosteroids immediately; treatment precedes biopsy because the other eye is at risk within days.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 50

src.question: A 74-year-old woman has sudden painless loss of vision in the left eye. She has had scalp tenderness when brushing her hair and aching in the jaw when chewing for three weeks. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is markedly raised. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Treatment precedes biopsy — the other eye is at risk within days.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Why open-angle glaucoma is missed. Loss is gradual and the other eye compensates, which is why it is found on screening rather than by symptoms.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 15

src.question: A 65-year-old woman is diagnosed with open-angle glaucoma. Why is she unlikely to have noticed anything?
src.key: Loss is gradual and the other eye compensates
src.explanation: Correct — which is why it is found on screening rather than by symptoms.

items.html: Papilledema versus optic neuritis. Acuity is preserved in papilledema and reduced in optic neuritis; papilledema is bilateral, while optic neuritis is usually unilateral with an afferent pupillary defect.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 45

src.question: A 31-year-old woman has bilateral disc swelling. What distinguishes papilledema from optic neuritis on examination?
src.key: Acuity is preserved in papilledema and reduced in optic neuritis
src.explanation: and papilledema is bilateral while optic neuritis is usually unilateral with an afferent pupillary defect.

items.html: Numbing drops for corneal abrasion. They should not be given to take home, because repeated use is toxic and delays healing, and it masks worsening infection.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 18

src.question: A 29-year-old man asks for a bottle of the numbing drops that relieved his corneal abrasion pain in the emergency department. Why should he not be given them?
src.key: Repeated use is toxic and delays healing
src.explanation: Correct — and it masks worsening infection.

items.html: Nystagmus present since birth. It warrants evaluation for a cause of poor vision, since congenital nystagmus often reflects an underlying visual deficit.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 4

src.question: A 3-week-old infant is noted to have rhythmic to-and-fro eye movements present since birth. What is the significance of nystagmus at this age?
src.key: It warrants evaluation for a cause of poor vision
src.explanation: Congenital nystagmus often reflects an underlying visual deficit.

items.section_title: 5.1 · The four rules that apply before any diagnosis
items.html: Embedded object in the eye. Leave it in place and arrange surgical repair, because it may be tamponading the wound and removal risks extruding intraocular contents.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 6

src.question: A 28-year-old man has a nail protruding from his left eye after a nail gun discharged. What should be done with the nail?
src.explanation: It may be tamponading the wound, and removal risks extruding intraocular contents.

also.explanation: It may be tamponading the wound, and removal can extrude intraocular contents.

also.key: Leave it in place and arrange surgical repair
also.explanation: It may be tamponading the wound, and removing it can extrude intraocular contents.

items.html: Blowout fracture with entrapment. Urgent surgical referral is required because entrapped muscle becomes ischemic and fibroses, and delay risks permanent restriction of eye movement.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 43

src.question: A 10-year-old girl has a white-eyed blowout fracture with entrapment. Why is urgent surgical referral required rather than routine review?
src.key: Entrapped muscle becomes ischemic and fibroses
src.explanation: Correct — delay risks permanent restriction of eye movement.

items.html: Hyphema management. Use upright positioning, a rigid shield and urgent ophthalmology review; keeping the head up lets the blood settle inferiorly and clear the visual axis.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 24

src.question: A 19-year-old man was hit in the eye by a paintball. Examination shows blood layered in the lower part of the anterior chamber occupying about a third of it. What is the most appropriate management?
src.key: Upright positioning, rigid shield and urgent ophthalmology review
src.explanation: Correct — keeping the head up lets the blood settle inferiorly and clear the visual axis.

items.html: Myopia risk factors. Family history and near work are risk factors, and trauma displacing the lens forward can cause myopia.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 18

src.question: Which are risk factors for myopia?
src.explanation: and trauma displacing the lens forward can cause it.

items.html: Orbital floor fracture without entrapment or ocular injury. Management is ice, analgesia and review in two to three days.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 41

src.question: A 26-year-old man has an orbital floor fracture with no entrapment and no ocular injury. What is the management?
src.key: Ice, analgesia and review in a few days
src.explanation: Two to three days.

items.html: Episcleritis. The inflamed tissue is the deep subconjunctival tissue, the episcleral layer.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 47

src.question: Which tissue is inflamed in episcleritis?
src.explanation: Correct — the episcleral layer.

items.html: Progression of pre-septal cellulitis. New pain on eye movement and mild proptosis mean the infection has progressed behind the orbital septum; painful restricted movement and proptosis indicate post-septal disease.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 53

src.question: A 7-year-old boy treated for pre-septal cellulitis returns after 48 hours with new pain on eye movement and mild proptosis. What has happened?
src.key: The infection has progressed behind the orbital septum
src.explanation: Correct — painful restricted movement and proptosis mean post-septal disease.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Lid laceration near the medial canthus. The canalicular drainage may be cut, and a missed canalicular injury leaves the person tearing for life.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 26

src.question: A 41-year-old woman has a lid laceration 4 mm from the medial canthus after a dog bite. Why does that location matter?
src.key: The canalicular drainage may be cut
src.explanation: Correct — a missed canalicular injury leaves the patient tearing for life.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Central retinal vein occlusion complication. Neovascular glaucoma is monitored for, because ischemia drives new vessel growth at the iris and angle.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 33

src.question: A 69-year-old man with a central retinal vein occlusion is being counseled. Which complication is he monitored for?
src.explanation: Correct — ischemia drives new vessel growth at the iris and angle.

items.html: Deferring lensectomy after full-thickness eye wall laceration. It is often deferred to let the hyphema and inflammation settle and to measure accurately for an implant.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 16

src.question: Why is lensectomy often deferred after a full-thickness eye wall laceration?
src.key: To let the hyphema and inflammation settle
src.explanation: And to measure accurately for an implant.

items.html: Treatment of amaurosis fugax from carotid emboli. Antiplatelet therapy is given for stroke risk, together with endarterectomy for the carotid source.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 8

src.question: A 66-year-old man has amaurosis fugax from carotid emboli. Which treatments are indicated?
src.explanation: Correct — antiplatelet therapy for stroke risk, and surgery for the carotid source. Aspirin and clopidogrel.

items.html: Lens correcting myopia. Myopia is corrected by a concave lens of negative diopter, which moves the focus back.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 18

src.question: Which statement correctly describes the lens that corrects myopia?
src.key: A concave lens, moving the focus back
src.explanation: Correct — negative diopter.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Cherry-red spot. It is the intact choroid showing through the fovea; the surrounding retina is pale from infarction, and the fovea has no inner retinal layers to become edematous.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 39

src.question: A 71-year-old woman has sudden painless loss of vision in the left eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula. What does the cherry-red spot represent?
src.key: Intact choroid showing through the fovea
src.explanation: The surrounding retina is pale from infarction; the fovea has no inner retinal layers to become edematous.

items.html: Deciding on cataract surgery. The decision is driven by the effect on daily functioning, that is, symptoms and function, rather than by an acuity threshold alone.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 37

src.question: A 73-year-old man has bilateral cataracts and vision of 6/18. He has stopped driving and finds reading difficult. What determines whether he is offered surgery?
src.key: The effect on his daily functioning
src.explanation: Correct — the decision is driven by symptoms and function rather than by an acuity threshold alone.

items.section_title: 5.1 · The four rules that apply before any diagnosis
items.html: Ocular trauma. Dilating the pupil must be avoided in any suspected ocular trauma, because it removes the pupil examination, one of the few windows onto the inside of the eye.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 6

src.question: A 36-year-old woman has a suspected open globe injury. Which action must be avoided in any suspected ocular trauma?
src.explanation: It removes the pupil examination, one of the few windows onto the inside of the eye.

also.explanation: It removes the pupil examination, one of the few windows onto the inside of the eye.

items.html: Imaging in suspected optic neuritis. Magnetic resonance of the brain and orbits is ordered, with and without contrast.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 23

src.question: A 29-year-old woman with suspected optic neuritis is referred for imaging. What is ordered?
src.key: Magnetic resonance of brain and orbits
src.explanation: With and without contrast.

items.html: Levels causing strabismus. The cause can lie in the brain, nerve, junction or muscle; causes are found at all four levels.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 29

src.question: A 6-year-old girl is referred with strabismus. At which levels of the visual motor system can the cause lie?
src.explanation: Correct — causes are found at all four levels.

items.html: Dry form of macular degeneration. About eighty percent of age-related macular degeneration is dry; the wet form accounts for the remaining twenty.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 11

src.question: What proportion of age-related macular degeneration is the dry form?
src.explanation: Correct — the wet form accounts for the remaining twenty.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Simple orbital contusion. When vision, pupils, eye movements and the globe are all normal, management is supportive: ice, analgesia and review if symptoms change.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 31

src.question: A 25-year-old man was elbowed in the eye during football. He has lid swelling and bruising, vision is 6/6, the pupils are equal and reactive, eye movements are full and the globe is intact. What is the most appropriate management?
src.key: Ice, analgesia and review if symptoms change
src.explanation: Correct — a simple orbital contusion with normal function needs supportive care.

items.html: Orbital floor fracture. Patients are advised not to blow the nose because it forces sinus air into the tissues; periorbital subcutaneous emphysema is a recognized feature of this fracture.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 43

src.question: A 33-year-old man with an orbital floor fracture is advised not to blow his nose. Why?
src.key: It forces sinus air into the tissues
src.explanation: Correct — periorbital subcutaneous emphysema, a recognized feature of orbital floor fracture.

items.html: Gradual painless vision loss in older patients. The three commonest causes, and so the top of the differential, are cataract, macular degeneration and open-angle glaucoma.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 11

src.question: A 70-year-old man reports gradual painless vision loss over two years. Which three diagnoses should be at the top of the differential?
src.key: Cataract, macular degeneration and open-angle glaucoma
src.explanation: Correct — the three commonest causes of gradual painless loss in this age group.

items.html: Mucous membrane pemphigoid. Chronic red, gritty eyes with progressive scarring of the lower palpebral conjunctiva, fornix shortening and oral erosions indicate it: progressive subconjunctival fibrosis with mucosal involvement elsewhere (the ocular form).
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 38

src.question: A 68-year-old woman has chronic red, gritty eyes with progressive scarring of the lower palpebral conjunctiva and shortening of the fornix. She also has oral erosions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Progressive subconjunctival fibrosis with mucosal involvement elsewhere. The ocular form.

items.html: Dacryocystitis needing admission. Fever, systemic illness or an unreliable patient move care to inpatient: intravenous therapy for 48 to 72 hours, then oral therapy to complete 10 to 14 days.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 25

src.question: A 71-year-old man with dacryocystitis is febrile, unwell and lives alone with no support. What is the appropriate management?
src.key: Admit for intravenous, then oral therapy
src.explanation: Correct — fever, systemic illness or unreliability all move him to inpatient care. Intravenous for 48 to 72 hours, then oral to complete 10 to 14 days.

items.html: Amaurosis fugax. A transient curtain-like loss of vision in one eye with full recovery is a transient ischemic attack of the eye, carries the same stroke risk, and calls for carotid imaging and urgent stroke workup.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 6

src.question: A 69-year-old man describes a curtain descending over the vision of his right eye, lasting about five minutes, with complete recovery. He has hypertension and smokes. Examination between episodes is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Carotid imaging and urgent stroke workup
src.explanation: It is a transient ischemic attack of the eye and carries the same stroke risk.

items.html: Recurrent lid nodule. A nodule that keeps recurring after being treated as a chalazion raises the possibility of sebaceous carcinoma; recurrent lesions, or one persisting beyond two to three months, are referred to rule this out.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 21

src.question: A 62-year-old man has had a lid nodule that has recurred three times in the same spot over eight months, each time treated as a chalazion. Why does the recurrence itself change the plan?
src.key: It raises the possibility of sebaceous carcinoma
src.explanation: Recurrent lesions, or one persisting beyond two to three months, are referred to rule this out.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Care strategies, adult and elderly Objective h
items.html: Neuro-ophthalmological work-up. After history and examination, head computed tomography or MRI is used if indicated.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 54

src.question: Which imaging is used, if indicated, in the general work-up of neuro-ophthalmological disorders?
src.explanation: if indicated after history and examination.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: First-order Horner syndrome. Brainstem stroke fits this level, along with spinal cord lesions above T1.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: A 52-year-old man has a first-order Horner syndrome. Which cause fits that level?
src.explanation: along with spinal cord lesions above T1.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Holmes-Adie syndrome. It is accompanied by absent deep tendon reflexes, often the Achilles or patellar reflex.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: Which systemic finding accompanies Holmes-Adie syndrome?
src.explanation: often the Achilles or patellar reflex.

items.section_title: 2.2 · The three pupillary pathways Objectives b, c, d
items.html: Light reflex, afferent limb. Afferent impulses travel along the second cranial nerve: retinal ganglion cells to the optic nerve and tracts.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 11

src.question: Along which cranial nerve do the afferent impulses of the light reflex travel?
src.explanation: retinal ganglion cells to the optic nerve and tracts.

items.section_title: 2.4 · Anisocoria — deciding which pupil is abnormal Objective f7
items.html: Pharmacologically dilated pupil. Anticholinergics such as atropine, ipratropium, scopolamine and glycopyrrolate can cause it, giving a large pupil that is unreactive to light.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: Which agents can cause a pharmacologically dilated pupil?
src.explanation: anticholinergics, giving a large pupil unreactive to light.

items.section_title: 2.4 · Anisocoria — deciding which pupil is abnormal Objective f7
items.html: Physiologic anisocoria. The size difference between the pupils is typically under about half a millimeter and is equal in light and dark.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: A 39-year-old woman has physiologic anisocoria. What size difference between her pupils is typical?
src.explanation: and equal in light and dark.

items.section_title: 2.4 · Anisocoria — deciding which pupil is abnormal Objective f7
items.html: Sympathomimetic versus anticholinergic pupil. A sympathomimetic-dilated pupil is only mildly enlarged, unlike the very large anticholinergic pupil.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: How does a sympathomimetic-dilated pupil differ from an anticholinergic one?
src.explanation: unlike the very large anticholinergic pupil.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Argyll Robertson pupils. Syphilis remains the classic association, but diabetes, alcohol, sarcoidosis and multiple sclerosis can also cause them.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 32

src.question: A 58-year-old man has Argyll Robertson pupils. Besides syphilis, what else can cause them?
src.explanation: though syphilis remains the classic association.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Horner syndrome anisocoria. The difference between the pupils is most evident within the first few seconds after the lights are dimmed, when a normal pupil would dilate rapidly and actively.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: How long after dimming the lights is the anisocoria of Horner syndrome most evident?
src.explanation: when a normal pupil would dilate rapidly and actively.

items.section_title: 2.3 · The accommodation reflex, and light-near dissociation Objective e
items.html: Pupillary light-near dissociation. It is defined by no reaction to light with a preserved reaction to near.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: What defines pupillary light-near dissociation?
src.key: No reaction to light, preserved reaction to near

items.html: Eyelid closure. The muscle that closes the eyelids, orbicularis oculi, is supplied by the seventh (facial) cranial nerve.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 48

src.question: Which nerve supplies the muscle that closes the eyelids?
src.explanation: the facial nerve supplies orbicularis oculi.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Apraclonidine in Horner syndrome. It dilates a Horner pupil through alpha-two greater than alpha-one activity, acting on a denervated, supersensitive pupil.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 28

src.question: Which receptor action explains why apraclonidine dilates a Horner pupil?
src.explanation: acting on a denervated, supersensitive pupil.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Adie pupil versus third nerve palsy. An Adie pupil has no ptosis and no extraocular weakness; a third nerve palsy also weakens the levator and extraocular muscles, giving ptosis and a down-and-out eye.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: A 30-year-old woman with a large tonic pupil has normal eyelid position and full eye movements. Which finding argues against a third nerve palsy?
src.key: No ptosis and no extraocular weakness
src.explanation: Correct — an Adie pupil has no other features of third nerve palsy, whereas a third nerve palsy also weakens the levator and extraocular muscles, giving ptosis and a down-and-out eye.

items.section_title: 2.8 · Pre- and post-chiasm lesions Objective g
items.html: Homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing. This pattern suggests a lesion of the occipital cortex; macular sparing is the cortical signature.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 52

src.question: A 70-year-old man has a left homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing after a stroke. Which location does that pattern suggest?
src.explanation: Macular sparing is the cortical signature.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Sixth nerve palsy. Binocular horizontal diplopia that worsens on gaze to one side, with under-abduction of that eye, means a sixth nerve palsy on that side: the lateral rectus abducts, and the deficit is on the side of gaze.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: A 34-year-old woman has binocular horizontal diplopia that worsens on looking to the left, and the left eye under-abducts. Which nerve is affected?
src.explanation: Lateral rectus abducts, and the deficit is on the side of gaze.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Patching in congenital palsy. Patching of a young child with a congenital palsy should be supervised by ophthalmology, especially under about five years of age.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: A parent asks about patching for a young child with a congenital palsy. What should the parent be told?
src.key: It should be supervised by ophthalmology
src.explanation: especially under about five years of age.

items.section_title: 2.4 · Anisocoria — deciding which pupil is abnormal Objective f7
items.html: Scopolamine patch mydriasis. A unilateral fixed dilated pupil after handling a scopolamine patch will resolve as the drug wears off; pharmacologic mydriasis is transient and needs no imaging.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: A nurse develops a unilateral fixed dilated pupil after handling a scopolamine patch. What should she be told?
src.key: It will resolve as the drug wears off
src.explanation: Pharmacologic mydriasis is transient and needs no imaging.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Head tilt in fourth nerve palsy. Tilting the head compensates for the weak muscle: the patient tilts away from the affected side to reduce the vertical deviation.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: A 38-year-old woman with a fourth nerve palsy asks why she keeps tilting her head. What is the best explanation?
src.key: Tilting compensates for the weak muscle
src.explanation: She tilts away from the affected side to reduce the vertical deviation.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Adie tonic pupil. It is often benign and asymptomatic, though photophobia and blurred near vision can occur.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: A 32-year-old woman is told she has an Adie tonic pupil. What is the most appropriate thing to tell her?
src.key: It is often benign and asymptomatic
src.explanation: though photophobia and blurred near vision can occur.

items.html: Fatigable bilateral ptosis with variable diplopia. This pattern points away from a structural palsy and toward myasthenia, so the next step is referral for neurologic evaluation.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 49

src.question: A 52-year-old woman has fatigable bilateral ptosis and variable diplopia. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: The pattern points away from a structural palsy and toward myasthenia.

items.html: Antiemetics in suspected open globe. They are given alongside analgesia because vomiting raises intraocular pressure; keeping the patient from straining protects the eye.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: Why are antiemetics given alongside analgesia in a suspected open globe?
src.explanation: Keeping the patient from straining protects the eye.

items.html: Ocular trauma epidemiology. Ocular trauma is the leading cause of monocular blindness in young adult men in the United States, so eye protection matters most for them.

src.question: Ocular trauma is the leading cause of monocular blindness in one population. Which statement correctly pairs that population with its counseling message?
src.key: Young adult men, so eye protection matters most

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Delayed facial laceration closure. A facial laceration may be left open for 24 hours before closure because the face is highly vascular, which is what permits the delay.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 27

src.question: Why may a facial laceration be left open for 24 hours before closure?
src.explanation: That vascularity is what permits the delay.

items.section_title: 5.1 · The four rules that apply before any diagnosis
items.html: Possible intraocular metal fragment. Computed tomography of the orbit is ordered, since it answers the question without moving the fragment.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: A metal fragment may be lodged in the eye after grinding. Which study is ordered?
src.explanation: It answers the question without moving the fragment.

items.html: Rust ring. A rust ring remaining after removal of a metallic foreign body is removed with a burr tip drill.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: A rust ring remains after a metallic foreign body is removed. How is it dealt with?
src.explanation: That is how a rust ring comes out.

items.html: Suspected open globe. Alongside the shield, give antiemetics, analgesia and tetanus, and obtain computed tomography; keeping the patient from straining protects the eye.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: Which set of measures accompanies the shield in a suspected open globe?
src.key: Antiemetics, analgesia, tetanus and computed tomography
src.explanation: Keeping the patient from straining protects the eye.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Partial-thickness lid laceration. One meeting none of the referral criteria is repaired at the initial site, with ophthalmology follow-up in 2 to 3 days; it does not need the specialist to close it.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 27

src.question: A partial-thickness lid laceration meets none of the referral criteria. How is it handled?
src.key: Repair there, ophthalmology in 2 to 3 days
src.explanation: It does not need the specialist to close it.

items.html: Suspected orbital fracture. Computed tomography of the orbits and midface is the imaging study for this fracture.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: A 40-year-old is suspected of an orbital fracture after a blow. Which imaging is ordered?
src.key: Computed tomography of the orbits and midface
src.explanation: That is the study for this fracture.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Periorbital swelling and ecchymosis after trauma. Beyond supportive care, brain trauma should be excluded, because the force that bruised the orbit reaches the brain.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 31

src.question: A 35-year-old has periorbital swelling and ecchymosis after a fall, with a normal globe and no hemorrhage within the orbit. Beyond supportive care, which is the most appropriate step?
src.explanation: The force that bruised the orbit reaches the brain.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Full-thickness lid laceration. Beyond repairing the lid, the globe underneath must be examined, because about two thirds of these lacerations come with a globe injury.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: A 21-year-old has a full-thickness upper lid laceration. Beyond repairing the lid, which is the most important step?
src.explanation: About two thirds of full-thickness lid lacerations come with one.

items.section_title: 5.1 · The four rules that apply before any diagnosis
items.html: Lid laceration with globe risk. The globe beneath is assessed before any lid repair, since two thirds of full-thickness lid lacerations have an accompanying globe injury.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: A 23-year-old has a laceration of the upper lid and a subconjunctival hemorrhage after being struck with a bottle. He is alert. Which is the most appropriate next step before any lid repair?
src.explanation: Two thirds of full-thickness lid lacerations have a globe injury with them.

items.html: Orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment. A facial trauma surgeon is contacted urgently, because an entrapped muscle can necrose if its blood supply is compromised.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: Computed tomography confirms an orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment in a 30-year-old. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Contact a facial trauma surgeon urgently
src.explanation: An entrapped muscle can necrose if its blood supply is compromised.

items.section_title: 5.1 · The four rules that apply before any diagnosis
items.html: Automatic imaging after facial trauma. Anticoagulation (such as warfarin) and confusion both make imaging automatic; computed tomography without contrast is the choice.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: A 45-year-old on warfarin fell and struck his face, and is now confused. His right eye is bruised. Which is the most appropriate imaging decision?
src.explanation: Both are on the list that makes imaging automatic.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Lid lacerations repairable in the emergency department. A superficial skin cut sparing the margin can be repaired there; partial-thickness lacerations meeting none of the referral criteria are repaired in the emergency department.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: Which of these lid lacerations can reasonably be repaired in the emergency department?
src.key: A superficial skin cut sparing the margin
src.explanation: Partial-thickness lacerations meeting none of the criteria are repaired there.

items.html: Macular involvement in retinal detachment. Field defects come first; a drop in central visual acuity indicates that the macula has become involved.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: Which symptom indicates the macula has become involved in a retinal detachment?
src.explanation: Field defects come first; central acuity falls with macular involvement.

items.html: Lensectomy timing in open globe injury. Lensectomy for a cut lens capsule is required but usually deferred from the globe repair, being performed later once hyphema and inflammation settle.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: A 36-year-old has a corneal laceration with a cut lens capsule and an opaque, swollen lens. When is lensectomy usually performed?
src.key: Later, once hyphema and inflammation settle
src.explanation: It is required but often deferred from the globe repair.

items.html: Globe rupture. A soft eye with massive hemorrhagic chemosis after blunt force is a globe rupture until proven otherwise; shield the eye and call ophthalmology.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: A 34-year-old man was struck in the right eye by a baseball. The lid is swollen, the conjunctiva is deeply hemorrhagic and the globe feels soft. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Shield the eye and call ophthalmology
src.explanation: A soft eye with massive hemorrhagic chemosis after blunt force is a globe rupture until proven otherwise.

items.html: Conjunctival foreign body. One visible on diffuse light examination is removed with a cotton-tipped applicator, since a conjunctival object lifts off with a swab.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: A conjunctival foreign body is visible on diffuse light examination in a 28-year-old. Which is the most appropriate removal method?
src.explanation: A conjunctival object lifts off with a swab.

items.html: Hyphema with sickle cell disease. Sickle cell anemia raises the risk of complications in hyphema, where a secondary hemorrhage can cause permanent visual loss.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25

src.question: A 15-year-old with sickle cell disease sustains a hyphema. Why does that history matter?
src.key: It raises the risk of complications
src.explanation: Sickle cell anemia increases the risk in hyphema, where a secondary hemorrhage can cause permanent visual loss.

items.section_title: 5.1 · The four rules that apply before any diagnosis
items.html: Periorbital penetrating injury. Penetration with metal or organic material carries tetanus risk, so confirm that tetanus immunization is up to date.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: A 29-year-old has a wooden splinter driven into the periorbital tissue while gardening. Beyond removing nothing and imaging appropriately, which additional step is required?
src.key: Confirm tetanus is up to date
src.explanation: Penetration with metal or organic material carries the risk.

items.html: Corneal abrasion at home. Give analgesia and a topical antibiotic; take-home anesthetic delays healing, masks worsening symptoms and can cause a corneal ulcer.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: A 27-year-old woman scratched her cornea removing a contact lens. Fluorescein confirms an abrasion. She asks for something for the pain to use at home. Which is the most appropriate response?
src.explanation: Take-home anesthetic delays healing, masks worsening symptoms and can cause a corneal ulcer.

items.html: Corneal ulcer referral. A corneal ulcer needs ophthalmology emergently, outranking keratitis's 24-hour window.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 61

src.question: How urgently does a corneal ulcer need ophthalmology?
src.explanation: Correct — an ulcer outranks keratitis's 24-hour window.

items.html: Entropion and ectropion. Slit lamp examination is required to assess corneal involvement, i.e. whether the cornea has been damaged.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: Which statement correctly describes the examination required for entropion and ectropion?
src.key: Slit lamp examination, to assess corneal involvement
src.explanation: Correct — the question is whether the cornea has been damaged.

items.html: Trichiasis from trachoma. It requires surgical treatment, because the lashes keep abrading the cornea until they are dealt with surgically.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: What does trichiasis from trachoma require?
src.explanation: Correct — the lashes keep abrading the cornea until they are dealt with surgically.

items.html: Doxycycline counseling. Avoid the sun (photosensitivity) and heed food and mineral interactions: take it with a full glass of water, stay upright, and separate it from antacids and from iron, calcium or magnesium.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: Which counseling points go with doxycycline?
src.key: Avoid the sun, and read which foods cannot be taken with it
src.explanation: Correct — photosensitivity plus food and mineral interactions; take it with a full glass of water, stay upright, and separate it from antacids and from iron, calcium or magnesium.

items.html: Corneal ulcer follow-up. Review is needed the next day after an anti-infective is started, and most ulcers heal over a two to three week course.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 61

src.question: A 41-year-old man has begun treatment for a corneal ulcer. What should he be told about follow-up and healing?
src.key: He needs review the next day, and most ulcers heal over two to three weeks
src.explanation: Correct — next-day follow-up after starting an anti-infective, with a two to three week course.
