items.html: Scleritis response to treatment. Decreased pain is the expected first sign of response and comes before any change in appearance, so an unchanged-looking eye is not failure.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: A 58-year-old man started treatment for scleritis three days ago. His eye still looks just as inflamed, but his pain is much better. How should this be interpreted?
src.key: This is the expected first sign of response — decreased pain comes before any change in appearance
src.explanation: Correct — pain settles first, so an unchanged-looking eye is not failure.

items.html: Mild dacryocystitis. In an afebrile, systemically well, reliable patient it is managed as an outpatient with oral antibiotics for ten days and warm compresses.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 25

src.question: A 62-year-old woman has a tender red swelling at the inner corner of her lower eyelid, with purulent material expressible from the lower punctum. She is afebrile, systemically well and reliable. Which is the most appropriate management?
src.key: Outpatient oral antibiotics for ten days with warm compresses
src.explanation: Correct — mild dacryocystitis in a well, reliable patient is managed as an outpatient.

items.html: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus. A dermatomal vesicular rash over the forehead and upper lid seen within the ideal 72-hour window calls for an oral antiviral now, plus referral for slit lamp examination and dilated fundoscopy.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 59

src.question: A 71-year-old woman presents 48 hours after a dermatomal vesicular rash appeared over her forehead and upper lid. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
src.key: Start an oral antiviral now and refer for slit lamp examination and dilated fundoscopy
src.explanation: Correct — within the ideal 72-hour window, and the eye still needs examining.

items.html: Posterior uveitis treatment. Topical treatment will not work; an intraocular corticosteroid injection may be required, the key management difference from anterior uveitis.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 65

src.question: A 45-year-old woman has blurred vision, floaters and a patch of missing vision in one eye, with no pain at all. Ophthalmology finds cells in the posterior vitreous and vitreous haze. Which statement about treatment is correct?
src.key: Topical treatment will not work here — an intraocular corticosteroid injection may be required
src.explanation: Correct — this is the key management difference from anterior uveitis.

items.html: Blepharoplasty coverage. Visual field testing is the assessment that determines coverage, because a demonstrated field deficit is what makes blepharoplasty a covered procedure.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 15

src.question: A 68-year-old man complains that his upper lids feel heavy and he is looking through his lashes. There are excess folds of skin over both upper lids. Which assessment most directly determines whether surgery will be covered?
src.explanation: Correct — a demonstrated field deficit is what makes blepharoplasty a covered procedure.

items.html: Corneal ulcer position. Prognosis follows both size and position relative to the visual axis; ulcers inside the visual axis carry a poorer outcome.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 56

src.question: A 50-year-old man has a moderate bacterial corneal ulcer that sits directly in front of his pupil. How does its position affect the outlook?
src.key: The prognosis is worse, because ulcers inside the visual axis carry a poorer outcome
src.explanation: Correct — prognosis follows both size and position relative to the visual axis.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Chronic open-angle glaucoma cause. Idiopathic optic nerve damage, from trabecular meshwork change with aging.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 15

src.question: A 63-year-old man has chronic open-angle glaucoma. How is its cause characterized?
src.explanation: from trabecular meshwork change with aging.

items.html: Retinal detachment symptoms. Vision changes with head position, which is unusual among causes of acute vision loss, because the detached retina moves.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 27

src.question: A 69-year-old man has a retinal detachment. Which feature of his visual symptoms is unusual among causes of acute vision loss?
src.explanation: because the detached retina moves.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. It affects people aged 55 years and older.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 49

src.question: A 74-year-old woman is being assessed for arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Which age group does it affect?

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. It typically affects people aged 40 to 60 years, accounting for 90 to 95 percent of cases.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 48

src.question: A 51-year-old man is diagnosed with non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Which age range does this form typically affect?
src.explanation: accounting for 90 to 95 percent of cases.

items.html: Optic neuritis course. Improvement within weeks, normal vision within a year, often without treatment.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 24

src.question: A 29-year-old man with optic neuritis asks how long recovery takes. What is the usual course?
src.key: Improvement within weeks, normal vision within a year
src.explanation: often without treatment.

items.html: Amaurosis fugax. Loss that descends over the field of one eye like a shade from above is attributed to retinal ischemia.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: A 68-year-old man describes vision descending over one eye like a shade from above. What is this attributed to?
src.explanation: when the loss descends over the field of one eye.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Central retinal artery occlusion. Anterior chamber paracentesis is performed to lower the intraocular pressure; fluid is withdrawn from the eye with a needle.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 40

src.question: A 72-year-old man has a central retinal artery occlusion. Why is anterior chamber paracentesis performed?
src.explanation: fluid is withdrawn from the eye with a needle.

items.html: Optic neuritis patient profile. Typically aged 18 to 45 and mostly female; about 75% are women.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 23

src.question: A 26-year-old woman is diagnosed with optic neuritis. Which patient profile is typical of this condition?
src.explanation: Correct; about 75% are women.

items.html: Glaucomatous optic disc damage. Defined by cupping, an excavated disc, with a raised cup-to-disc ratio.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: A 66-year-old woman has her discs examined for glaucoma. Which change defines the damage?
src.explanation: with a raised cup-to-disc ratio.

items.html: Dry macular degeneration. Defined by drusen, pigment change and atrophy. Neovascular bleeding defines the wet form instead.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 11

src.question: A 78-year-old woman has macular changes but no bleeding. Which findings define the dry form?
src.explanation: Neovascular bleeding defines the wet form instead.

items.html: Amblyopia treated late. An adult may have good acuity but struggle with 3D films because stereo vision never developed; the brain still uses one eye at a time.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 33

src.question: An adult treated late for childhood amblyopia has good acuity but struggles with 3D films. Why?
src.explanation: The brain still uses one eye at a time.

items.html: Amblyopia mechanism. The brain favors one eye and the other fails to develop. Strabismus, refractive difference or deprivation all do this.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 33

src.question: A 3-year-old girl has one eye with a much stronger prescription than the other. How does amblyopia arise?
src.key: The brain favors one eye and the other fails to develop
src.explanation: Strabismus, refractive difference or deprivation all do this.

items.html: Astigmatism. Uneven curvature gives several focal points, so no single point focus forms, causing blur at every distance.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 20

src.question: A 24-year-old woman has blur at every distance that glasses correct. Why does astigmatism do this?
src.key: Uneven curvature gives several focal points
src.explanation: so no single point focus forms.

items.html: Who needs a yearly ophthalmologist. A patient with diabetes needs a yearly ophthalmologist rather than an optometrist, because a medical eye problem needs the medical specialist.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: Which patient most needs a yearly ophthalmologist rather than an optometrist?
src.explanation: A medical eye problem needs the medical specialist.

items.html: Farsightedness. A convex lens corrects it because it converges light onto the retina; the farsighted eye focuses behind the retina.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: A 45-year-old man is farsighted. Why does a convex lens correct him?
src.key: It converges light onto the retina
src.explanation: His eye focuses behind the retina.

items.html: Patching in amblyopia. A patch over the good eye makes the weaker eye work; the stronger eye otherwise does everything.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: A father asks why his son must wear a patch over his good eye. What do you explain?
src.key: It makes the weaker eye work
src.explanation: The stronger eye otherwise does everything.

items.html: Dense macular scar from previous bleeding. This is wet macular degeneration, because it began with neovascular bleeding. The scar is the end stage of the wet process.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 11

src.question: An 86-year-old man has a dense scar at the macula from previous bleeding. Which form of macular degeneration is this?
src.key: Wet, because it began with neovascular bleeding
src.explanation: The scar is the end stage of the wet process.

items.html: Wet macular degeneration treatment. Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection, with photodynamic therapy and laser as alternatives.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 14

src.question: An 83-year-old woman is confirmed to have wet macular degeneration. Which treatment is offered?
src.explanation: with photodynamic therapy and laser as alternatives.

items.html: Untreated retinoblastoma. It is almost always fatal, which is why referral cannot wait.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: A family asks what happens if retinoblastoma goes untreated. What is the answer?
src.explanation: which is why referral cannot wait.

items.html: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension workup. Imaging with venography comes first; when it is normal, the next step is lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure, which confirms the diagnosis.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 5

src.question: A 27-year-old woman with obesity has six weeks of headache, pulsatile tinnitus and papilledema. Brain imaging with venography is normal. What is the next step?
src.key: Lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure
src.explanation: Imaging first, then the pressure measurement that confirms it.

items.html: Cupped discs on routine examination. Refer to ophthalmology for assessment; good central vision does not exclude damage.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: A 65-year-old woman is found to have cupped discs on a routine examination but sees well. What happens next?
src.explanation: Good central vision does not exclude damage.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Treated choroidal melanoma follow-up. Surveillance for liver metastasis, because the liver is where it goes.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: A 64-year-old man treated for choroidal melanoma asks what follow-up he needs. What do you tell him?
src.explanation: The liver is where it goes.

items.html: Ptosis causes. Horner syndrome and third nerve palsy both drop the lid, and each also disturbs the pupil, so ptosis appears alongside anisocoria.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 2

src.question: Which pair of neuro-ophthalmological conditions produces ptosis?
src.key: Horner syndrome and third nerve palsy
src.explanation: Correct — both drop the lid, and each also disturbs the pupil, so ptosis appears alongside anisocoria.

items.html: Wet macular degeneration with acute distortion and central gray patch. Straight lines distort, with subretinal fluid and hemorrhage at the macula. Give urgent referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy; the wet form is treatable and the window matters.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 14

src.question: An 80-year-old man reports that over the past week straight lines have become sharply distorted in the right eye and a gray patch has appeared in the center of his vision. Fundoscopy shows subretinal fluid and hemorrhage at the macula. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Urgent referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy
src.explanation: The wet form is treatable and the window matters.

items.html: Globe rupture sites. Ruptures commonly occur behind the muscle insertions, especially superonasally, and also along incisions from earlier intraocular surgery and at the lamina cribrosa.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 17

src.question: A 52-year-old man sustains a globe rupture from an airbag. Where do such ruptures commonly occur?
src.explanation: especially superonasally, and also along incisions from earlier intraocular surgery and at the lamina cribrosa.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Giant cell arteritis with vision loss. Start treatment today rather than waiting for the biopsy, because the fellow eye can be lost within days.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 51

src.question: A 78-year-old man with giant cell arteritis and vision loss in one eye asks why he must start treatment today rather than wait for the biopsy. What is the reason?
src.key: The fellow eye can be lost within days

items.html: Metallic corneal foreign body with rust ring. Remove it and the rust ring, then give antibiotics. The rust ring is removed too, as it perpetuates inflammation.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 21

src.question: A 33-year-old man has a metallic foreign body embedded in the cornea with a surrounding rust ring, 24 hours after grinding. Vision is 6/9. What is the most appropriate management?
src.key: Remove it and the rust ring, then antibiotics
src.explanation: Correct — the rust ring is removed too, as it perpetuates inflammation.

items.html: Transient monocular vision loss lasting minutes. The mechanism is transient retinal ischemia, usually embolic, most often from carotid atheroma.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 5

src.question: A 72-year-old woman describes transient monocular vision loss lasting minutes. What is the underlying mechanism?
src.explanation: Correct — most often from carotid atheroma.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Black eye after a punch. A relative afferent pupillary defect makes it more than a simple contusion; it indicates optic nerve involvement and changes the urgency entirely.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 33

src.question: A 38-year-old man has a black eye after being punched. Which finding would make this more than a simple contusion?
src.explanation: Correct — that indicates optic nerve involvement and changes the urgency entirely.

items.html: Neonate with marked bilateral lid edema, copious purulent discharge and a preauricular node. Hospitalize and give systemic ceftriaxone as a single dose, with specialty consultation; the untreated risk is corneal perforation.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 41

src.question: A 3-day-old neonate has marked bilateral lid edema and copious purulent discharge. A palpable preauricular node is present. What is the most appropriate management?
src.explanation: with specialty consultation — the untreated risk is corneal perforation. A single dose.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Third nerve palsy with a normal, reactive pupil. A normal pupil in ptosis with the eye deviated down and out suggests a microvascular ischemic cause. Pupillary fibers run peripherally and are spared by ischemia but compressed by an aneurysm.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 41

src.question: A 66-year-old man with diabetes has ptosis and an eye deviated down and out, but the pupil is normal in size and reactive. What does the pupil finding suggest about the cause?
src.explanation: The pupillary fibers run peripherally and are spared by ischemia but compressed by an aneurysm.

items.html: Corneal laceration with iris prolapse. Do not attempt repositing the prolapsed iris; manipulation risks further extrusion and infection. Shield the eye and refer in the emergency department.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 15

src.question: A 30-year-old man was struck by a shard of glass. Examination shows a full-thickness corneal laceration with iris prolapsing through it. What must NOT be attempted?
src.explanation: Correct — manipulation risks further extrusion and infection; shield and refer. In the emergency department.

items.html: Optic neuritis with demyelinating lesions on imaging. Neurology referral with corticosteroids follows; steroids are given if a demyelinating cause is found. Neuro-ophthalmology is equally appropriate.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 24

src.question: A 33-year-old woman with optic neuritis is found to have two demyelinating lesions on imaging. What follows?
src.explanation: Correct — steroids if a demyelinating cause is found. Neuro-ophthalmology is equally appropriate.

items.section_title: 3.1 · The four questions that separate these diagnoses
items.html: Assessing acute vision loss. The initial assessment turns on four questions: one or both eyes, duration, pain, and a description of the symptoms.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 4

src.question: A patient presents with acute vision loss. Which four questions does the initial assessment turn on?
src.key: One or both eyes, duration, pain, and a description
src.explanation: Ask whether one or both eyes were affected, how long it lasted, whether there was pain, and for a specific description of the symptoms.

items.html: Seventh nerve palsy and lid position. Seventh nerve palsy causes ectropion, with the lower lid margin turned outward, watering and a red, exposed inner lid surface. Of the two malpositions, it causes ectropion only.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 13

src.question: A 71-year-old woman has watering of the left eye and a red, exposed inner lid surface. Examination shows the lower lid margin turned outward. She had a facial nerve palsy last year with incomplete recovery. What is the most likely explanation?
src.explanation: Of the two malpositions, a seventh nerve palsy causes ectropion only.

items.html: After removing a superficial corneal foreign body. Check that there is no deeper injury, because a superficial fragment can accompany a penetrating one.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 22

src.question: A 34-year-old welder has a superficial corneal foreign body removed. What must be checked before he leaves?
src.key: That there is no deeper injury
src.explanation: Correct — a superficial fragment can accompany a penetrating one. No second, penetrating injury.

items.html: Herpes simplex keratitis prognosis. Good, though recurrences are common.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 59

src.question: What is the prognosis of herpes simplex keratitis?

items.html: Bacterial conjunctivitis risk groups. Immunocompromised, elderly, children and contact lens wearers are at particular risk. Neonates are a separate concern, where gonococcal infection is the worry.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 41

src.question: Which patients are at particular risk of bacterial conjunctivitis?
src.key: Immunocompromised, elderly, children, contact lens wearers
src.explanation: Neonates are a separate concern, where gonococcal infection is the worry.

items.html: Post-septal cellulitis. All post-septal disease is admitted for intravenous antibiotics and imaging; computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses defines the extent.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 53

src.question: A 9-year-old girl has a swollen red eyelid, proptosis, pain on eye movement and diplopia. Temperature 39.0°C. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Admit for intravenous antibiotics and imaging
src.explanation: All post-septal disease is admitted, and imaging defines the extent. Computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses.

items.html: Yellowish plaques near the inner canthus. Initial workup is lipid, diabetes and liver blood tests: a serum lipid profile, fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1C, and liver function tests. The lesion is a marker of the metabolic issue that is treated.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 17

src.question: A 54-year-old woman has painless, oval yellowish plaques on both upper lids near the inner canthus. Vision is normal. What is the most appropriate initial workup?
src.key: Lipid, diabetes and liver blood tests
src.explanation: Order a serum lipid profile, fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1C, and liver function tests; the lesion is a marker of the metabolic issue that is treated.

items.html: Suspected retinal detachment with a poor fundus view. Ocular ultrasound is more sensitive than fundoscopy, and it also types the detachment.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 28

src.question: A 57-year-old woman has a suspected retinal detachment but the view of the fundus is poor. Which investigation is more sensitive than fundoscopy?
src.explanation: Correct — and it types the detachment as well.

items.html: Corticosteroids in painful lid swelling of unclear cause. Infection must be reasonably excluded first; the alternative path is empiric oral antibiotics for 24 hours with reassessment.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 23

src.question: A 41-year-old woman has painful swelling of the outer upper lid and the cause is not yet clear. Why must corticosteroids not be started immediately?
src.key: Infection must be reasonably excluded first
src.explanation: Correct — empiric oral antibiotics for 24 hours with reassessment is the alternative path.

items.html: Hyphema screening. Sickle cell testing is particularly important in a patient of African ancestry; sickling in the anterior chamber obstructs outflow and raises pressure at lower blood volumes.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 25

src.question: A 15-year-old boy of African ancestry has a traumatic hyphema. Which screening test is particularly important in his case?
src.explanation: Sickling in the anterior chamber obstructs outflow and raises pressure at lower blood volumes.

items.html: Improved near vision in cataract. A myopic shift from nuclear sclerosis ('second sight') explains it: the hardening lens increases its refractive power.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 36

src.question: A 71-year-old man reports gradually blurring distance vision and increasing glare from oncoming headlights at night. He mentions he no longer needs his reading glasses. What explains the improvement in near vision?
src.key: A myopic shift from nuclear sclerosis
src.explanation: Correct — 'second sight'. The hardening lens increases its refractive power.

items.html: Allergic conjunctivitis unresponsive to topical treatment. The diagnosis may be wrong, so refer; symptoms usually settle as allergen levels fall.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 35

src.question: A 19-year-old man's allergic conjunctivitis has not responded to topical treatment. What does that suggest?
src.key: The diagnosis may be wrong, so refer
src.explanation: Correct — symptoms usually settle as allergen levels fall.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Central retinal vein occlusion. Look for hypertension, diabetes and hyperviscosity; the venous side reflects systemic vascular and rheological disease.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 34

src.question: A 62-year-old woman has a central retinal vein occlusion. Which systemic conditions should be sought?
src.explanation: Correct — the venous side reflects systemic vascular and rheological disease.

items.section_title: 4.11 · The differentials — what else looks like this
items.html: Ocular trauma red flag. A relative afferent pupillary defect converts a routine review into an emergency referral, because it indicates optic nerve compromise.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 3

src.question: Which finding after ocular trauma converts a routine review into an emergency referral?
src.explanation: Correct — it indicates optic nerve compromise.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Sixth nerve palsy. It is a false localizing sign because of its long intracranial course; the palsy does not indicate where the lesion is, since raised pressure anywhere can affect it.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 46

src.question: A 29-year-old woman with headaches and papilledema is found to have a sixth nerve palsy. Why is this described as a false localizing sign?
src.explanation: Correct — the palsy does not indicate where the lesion is. Raised pressure anywhere can affect it.

items.section_title: 2.8 · Pre- and post-chiasm lesions Objective g
items.html: Monocular field defect. The lesion lies anterior to the chiasm; a monocular defect localizes pre-chiasmal.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 25

src.question: A field defect is found to be MONOCULAR. Where must the lesion be?
src.explanation: Correct — a monocular defect localizes pre-chiasmal.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Third nerve palsy causes. Severe head trauma is a cause, alongside microvascular disease and aneurysm.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 40

src.question: A 70-year-old man has a third nerve palsy after a fall with loss of consciousness. Which cause is most likely?
src.explanation: alongside microvascular disease and aneurysm.

items.html: Early-onset nystagmus. It is usually asymptomatic if acquired before age eight, which is why onset age matters.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 3

src.question: A 30-year-old woman developed nystagmus at age three and has no symptoms. What is true of symptoms in early-onset nystagmus?
src.key: It is usually asymptomatic if acquired before age eight
src.explanation: which is why onset age matters.

items.section_title: 2.2 · The three pupillary pathways Objectives b, c, d
items.html: Opioid toxicity. The features that matter clinically are reduced consciousness and respiratory depression; the miosis is a clue rather than the danger.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 12

src.question: A 27-year-old woman has opioid toxicity. Which two features actually matter clinically?
src.explanation: Correct; the miosis is a clue rather than the danger.

items.section_title: 2.2 · The three pupillary pathways Objectives b, c, d
items.html: Pupillary muscles. The iris sphincter constricts and the radial muscle dilates, producing miosis and mydriasis respectively.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: Which statement correctly pairs the pupillary muscles with their actions?
src.key: Iris sphincter constricts, radial muscle dilates
src.explanation: miosis and mydriasis respectively.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Absent anhidrosis with ptosis and miosis. It does not exclude the diagnosis, since it depends on lesion level: the triad may be incomplete depending where along the pathway the lesion sits.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 28

src.question: A 55-year-old woman has ptosis and miosis on the left with no anhidrosis. Does the absent anhidrosis exclude the diagnosis?
src.key: No, it depends on lesion level
src.explanation: The triad may be incomplete depending where along the pathway the lesion sits.

also.key: It depends where the lesion sits
also.explanation: The triad may be incomplete depending on the level along the pathway.

items.html: Monocular or asymmetric nystagmus. Refer for work-up; it is a concerning, non-physiologic pattern.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 5

src.question: A 22-year-old woman has new asymmetric nystagmus in one eye only. What is the next step?
src.explanation: Monocular or asymmetric nystagmus is a concerning, non-physiologic pattern that needs referral and work-up.

items.section_title: 2.2 · The three pupillary pathways Objectives b, c, d
items.html: Naloxone reversal. Naloxone may need repeating, because it lasts about two hours and respiratory depression can return.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 12

src.question: A patient is discharged after naloxone reversal. Which point about naloxone matters most?
src.explanation: It lasts about two hours, so respiratory depression can return.

items.html: Nystagmus in infants and young children. It warrants referral for work-up.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 5

src.question: A 3-month-old infant is noted to have nystagmus. What is the next step?
src.explanation: Infants and young children with nystagmus warrant referral.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Adie pupil. Dilute pilocarpine drops support the diagnosis: the denervated pupil is supersensitive and constricts.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: A 31-year-old woman has a unilateral large, poorly reactive pupil. Which bedside test is used to support an Adie pupil?
src.explanation: The denervated pupil is supersensitive and constricts.

items.html: Globe rupture risk. Previous intraocular surgery makes rupture more likely at lower force, because old incisions leave a permanent weak point.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: Which history makes globe rupture more likely at lower force?
src.explanation: Old incisions leave a permanent weak point.

also.key: Old incisions leave a permanent weak point
also.explanation: Prior intraocular surgery lowers the force needed.

items.html: Lens capsule laceration. The lens becomes hydrated, edematous and opaque, as aqueous entering the capsule clouds it.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: A laceration has cut the lens capsule. What happens to the lens?
src.key: It becomes hydrated, edematous and opaque
src.explanation: Aqueous entering the capsule clouds it.

items.html: Vertical linear corneal scratches. Evert the upper lid to find the object; vertical linear defects mean it is in the tarsal conjunctiva of the upper lid, scraping with each blink.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: A patient who was grinding metal has vertical linear scratches across the cornea. What does that indicate?
src.key: Evert the upper lid to find the object
src.explanation: Vertical linear defects mean it is in the tarsal conjunctiva of the upper lid.

also.explanation: Vertical linear defects mean the object is under the upper lid, scraping with each blink.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Orbital contusion versus periorbital hematoma. Contusion has no hemorrhage; the hematoma bleeds in the orbit. The septum is what keeps the contusion in front of the eye.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 31

src.question: What distinguishes an orbital contusion from a periorbital hematoma?
src.key: Contusion has no hemorrhage; the hematoma bleeds in the orbit
src.explanation: The septum is what keeps the contusion in front of the eye.

items.html: Hyphema. A layer of blood with a fluid level in the anterior chamber is hyphema, and it can itself indicate an open globe; it is not always an isolated injury.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 24

src.question: A 16-year-old was hit in the eye by a paintball. There is a layer of blood across the lower anterior chamber with a visible fluid level. Which statement about the most likely diagnosis is correct?
src.key: Hyphema, and it can itself indicate an open globe
src.explanation: It is not always an isolated injury.

items.html: Corneal rust ring. A rust ring from iron or copper is removed with a battery-operated burr.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: A metallic corneal foreign body is removed from a 45-year-old, leaving a brown ring in the stroma. Which is the most appropriate management of that ring?
src.key: Remove it with a battery-operated burr
src.explanation: A rust ring from iron or copper comes out with a burr.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Lid laceration referral. A laceration through the lid margin goes to ophthalmology, because margin involvement is one of the explicit referral criteria.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: A 33-year-old has a 1 centimeter laceration running through the lower lid margin after a dog bite. Which is the most appropriate disposition?
src.key: Ophthalmology, because the lid margin is involved
src.explanation: Margin involvement is one of the explicit referral criteria.

items.html: Hyphema discharge instructions. Avoid aspirin, antiplatelets and straining, since both raise the risk of a secondary hemorrhage.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25

src.question: A 20-year-old with a hyphema is being discharged after admission. Which instruction matters most?
src.explanation: Both raise the risk of a secondary hemorrhage.

items.html: Retinal detachment urgency. A fresh detachment must be seen by an ophthalmologist within 24 hours; the referral is immediate.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: A 55-year-old with a fresh retinal detachment asks how urgently she needs to be seen. Which is the most accurate response?
src.explanation: The referral is immediate.

items.html: Hospitalizing pre-septal cellulitis. Admit for moderate to severe or toxic disease, concern for poor compliance, a child of five years or younger, or no improvement after oral antibiotics were started.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 53

src.question: Which patients with PRE-septal cellulitis are hospitalized?
src.key: Moderate to severe or toxic disease, concern for poor compliance, a child of five years or younger, or no improvement after oral antibiotics were started
src.explanation: Correct — these are the four admission criteria, with five years as the pediatric cut-off.

items.html: Chalazion versus hordeolum. Tenderness separates them: the hordeolum is tender and the chalazion is not.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 20

src.question: Which single examination finding separates a chalazion from a hordeolum?
src.key: Tenderness — the hordeolum is tender and the chalazion is not
src.explanation: Correct — tenderness is the discriminating sign.

items.html: Scleritis referral. Refer to ophthalmology urgently, because the sclera is at risk of perforation and may need a surgical patch.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: Which statement correctly describes the urgency of ophthalmology referral for scleritis?
src.key: Urgently — the sclera is at risk of perforation and may need a surgical patch
src.explanation: Correct — the urgency follows from the perforation risk.

items.html: Corneal ulcer on examination. The patient resists opening the affected eye, because of photophobia and foreign body sensation.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 60

src.question: Which examination behavior is characteristic of a corneal ulcer?
src.key: The patient resists opening the affected eye
src.explanation: Correct — photophobia and foreign body sensation make the patient resist.

items.html: Hordeolum referral. Refer to ophthalmology if persistent, for example no improvement in two weeks, for incision and drainage.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: When is a hordeolum referred to ophthalmology, and for what?
src.key: If persistent — for example no improvement in two weeks — for incision and drainage
src.explanation: Correct — that is the threshold and the procedure.

items.html: Inflammatory dacryoadenitis. Treat with oral corticosteroids, with a response expected within 48 hours.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 23

src.question: Which statement correctly describes the treatment of INFLAMMATORY dacryoadenitis and its expected response?
src.key: Corticosteroids, with a response expected within 48 hours
src.explanation: Correct — corticosteroids, with response inside 48 hours.

also.key: Oral corticosteroids, with a response expected within 48 hours
also.explanation: Correct — that is the agent and the response window for inflammatory dacryoadenitis.

items.html: Posterior versus anterior uveitis course. Posterior uveitis develops a lot more slowly and may last several years, though it can also turn acute and threaten vision.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 65

src.question: How does the time course of posterior uveitis compare with anterior uveitis?
src.key: It develops a lot more slowly and may last several years
src.explanation: Correct — it develops more slowly and can persist for years, though it can also turn acute and threaten vision.

items.html: Xanthelasma prognosis. Recurrences are common even after effective local treatment, whatever the local treatment.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: What is the prognosis of locally treated xanthelasma?
src.key: Recurrences are common even after effective local treatment
src.explanation: Correct — recurrence is common whatever the local treatment.

also.key: Even after effective local treatment, recurrences are common
also.explanation: Correct — recurrence is common even after effective local treatment.

items.html: Pinguecula versus pterygium. The pterygium extends into the cornea; the pinguecula does not involve it. Corneal involvement is the whole distinction.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 27

src.question: What separates a pinguecula from a pterygium?
src.key: The pterygium extends into the cornea; the pinguecula does not involve it
src.explanation: Correct — corneal involvement is the whole distinction; pterodactyls fly into the cornea and penguins cannot.

items.html: Demonstrating a corneal abrasion. Instill fluorescein and examine under a Wood's lamp with ultraviolet light; this surface fluorescein examination detects abrasions, ulcers and foreign bodies.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: A 35-year-old man may have a corneal abrasion after a fingernail injury. Which examination will best demonstrate it?
src.key: Instill fluorescein and examine under a Wood's lamp with ultraviolet light
src.explanation: Correct — the surface fluorescein examination detects abrasions, ulcers and foreign bodies.

items.html: Ectropion treatment. Surgery is the definitive treatment, since only surgery restores lid position permanently; lubrication only protects the surface in the meantime.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: A 77-year-old woman with ectropion asks what will actually fix it. What is the most accurate answer?
src.key: Surgery is the definitive treatment; lubrication only protects the surface in the meantime
src.explanation: Correct — only surgery restores lid position permanently.

items.html: Unexplained bright red patch on the sclera. Take a careful history and check blood pressure; history is the priority, and an unexplained bleed warrants a blood pressure check.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: A 59-year-old man has a painless bright red patch on the white of one eye with no obvious precipitant and no medication history to explain it. Vision, pupil and cornea are all normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Take a careful history and check his blood pressure
src.explanation: Correct — history is the priority, and an unexplained bleed warrants a blood pressure check.

items.html: Recurrent uveitis with systemic features. Recurrent uveitis with suggestive systemic features warrants a thorough systemic evaluation for an underlying autoimmune condition.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 63

src.question: A 44-year-old man has had three separate episodes of anterior uveitis in two years and reports joint pain and lower back stiffness. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Thorough systemic evaluation for an underlying autoimmune condition
src.explanation: Correct — recurrent uveitis with suggestive systemic features warrants a full evaluation.

items.html: Yellowish plaques on the inner upper eyelids. Workup is a serum lipid profile, together with tests for diabetes mellitus and liver function; the plaques are a marker of an underlying metabolic disorder.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: A 47-year-old woman has soft yellowish oval plaques on the inner aspect of both upper eyelids. They are asymptomatic. Which workup is most appropriate?
src.key: Serum lipid profile, together with tests for diabetes mellitus and liver function
src.explanation: Correct — the plaques are a marker of an underlying metabolic disorder.

items.html: Chlamydial conjunctivitis. Beyond treating the eye, arrange evaluation for other sexually transmitted infections and notify partners for evaluation; the eye finding is a sentinel for a usually asymptomatic urogenital infection.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: A 23-year-old woman has been diagnosed with chlamydial conjunctivitis confirmed on conjunctival testing. Beyond treating her eye, which is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Arrange evaluation for other sexually transmitted infections and notify her partners for evaluation
src.explanation: Correct — the eye finding is a sentinel for a usually asymptomatic urogenital infection.

items.html: Nasal-tip vesicle (Hutchinson sign). It indicates nasociliary branch involvement, and therefore a higher risk of ocular involvement.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 58

src.question: A 68-year-old man has a painful vesicular rash over his forehead and one upper eyelid that stops sharply at the midline, and a vesicle on the tip of his nose. What does the nasal-tip lesion indicate?
src.key: Nasociliary branch involvement, and therefore a higher risk of ocular involvement
src.explanation: Correct — Hutchinson sign, and its significance is the ocular risk.

items.html: Curtain coming down over vision. This description is a warning sign because more than one condition uses it; it fits amaurosis fugax and retinal detachment.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: A 62-year-old man says a curtain came down over his vision. Why is this description a warning sign?
src.key: More than one condition uses it
src.explanation: Correct; it fits amaurosis fugax and retinal detachment.

items.html: Dry to wet macular degeneration. In the wet form, new vessels from the choroid bleed into retina, and the blood organizes into a scar.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 11

src.question: An 84-year-old man's dry macular degeneration turns wet. What has changed?
src.key: New vessels from the choroid bleed into retina
src.explanation: and the blood organizes into a scar.

items.html: Unilateral amblyopia. It is defined by two or more lines of difference between the eyes on best corrected acuity.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: A 7-year-old girl reads 20/50 with one eye and 20/30 with the other. What defines unilateral amblyopia?
src.key: Two or more lines of difference
src.explanation: on best corrected acuity.

items.html: Cataract that blocks the retinal exam. Surgery is needed to see behind it, because the cataract blocks diagnosis of other eye disease.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: A 66-year-old woman has a cataract and cannot have her retina examined because of it. Does that change the plan?
src.key: Yes, surgery is needed to see behind it
src.explanation: It blocks diagnosis of other eye disease.

items.html: Retinal detachment with the macula still attached. Central vision is salvageable before the macula goes, so macula-on detachment is the more urgent repair.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 29

src.question: A 61-year-old woman has a retinal detachment with the macula still attached. Why does that detail change the urgency?
src.key: Central vision is salvageable before the macula goes
src.explanation: Correct — macula-on detachment is the more urgent repair.

items.html: Corneal infiltrate with epithelial defect and hypopyon. Urgent referral for scraping and antibiotics is the next step. A hypopyon indicates significant intraocular inflammation and the eye is at risk; treatment is intensive topical antibiotics after corneal scraping.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 61

src.question: A 45-year-old woman has a painful red eye with a 2 mm white corneal infiltrate, an overlying epithelial defect and a small hypopyon. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Urgent referral for scraping and antibiotics
src.explanation: A hypopyon indicates significant intraocular inflammation and the eye is at risk. Intensive topical antibiotics after corneal scraping.

items.html: Corneal abrasion that worsens. Worsening pain and a white spot on the cornea mean a corneal ulcer has developed. This is why abrasions are re-examined, and why anesthetic drops are never sent home.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: A 42-year-old treated for a corneal abrasion three days ago returns with worsening pain and a white spot on the cornea. Which is the most likely explanation?
src.explanation: This is why abrasions are re-examined, and why anesthetic drops are never sent home.

items.html: Episcleritis. The bedside test is to instill 2.5 percent phenylephrine and look for blanching of the vessels after 15 minutes; episcleral vessels blanch, and mild painless sectoral redness fits episcleritis.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 48

src.question: A 34-year-old woman has two days of mild ache and a sectoral patch of redness in one eye, with no discharge and no photophobia. Which bedside test best confirms the diagnosis?
src.key: Instill 2.5 percent phenylephrine and look for blanching of the vessels after 15 minutes
src.explanation: Correct — episcleral vessels blanch; the mild painless sectoral redness fits episcleritis.

items.html: Types of retinal detachment. Rhegmatogenous, traction and serous; the serous form is also called exudative.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: A 70-year-old woman is told she has one of the three types of retinal detachment. What are the three types?
src.explanation: Correct; the serous form is also called exudative.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Frequency of retinal vascular occlusions. Vein occlusion is more common than central retinal artery occlusion.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 32

src.question: A 61-year-old woman asks which retinal vascular occlusion is seen more often. What should she be told?
src.explanation: more common than central retinal artery occlusion.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Central retinal artery occlusion. It causes sudden profound painless loss of vision, with a pale, swollen retina and a cherry-red spot at the fovea.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 39

src.question: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has profound painless loss of vision in the right eye that came on over a few seconds. He can only count fingers. The retina is pale and swollen with a cherry-red spot at the fovea. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Sudden profound loss with the cherry-red fovea.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Arterial versus venous retinal occlusion on fundoscopy. Arterial occlusion shows pallor with a cherry-red spot at the fovea rather than hemorrhages.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 39

src.question: A 73-year-old man loses vision in one eye. Which finding separates arterial from venous retinal occlusion on fundoscopy?
src.key: A cherry-red spot rather than hemorrhages
src.explanation: Correct; the artery gives pallor with a cherry-red fovea.

items.html: Most common form of glaucoma. Primary open-angle glaucoma is the most common form, and it is characteristically painless and slow.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: A 70-year-old man is told he has glaucoma. Which form is most common?
src.explanation: and it is characteristically painless and slow.

items.html: Treatment of cataract. Surgery to replace the lens, deferred until the cataract interferes with daily activities.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 39

src.question: A 77-year-old man asks what will fix his cataract. What is the answer?
src.explanation: deferred until it interferes with daily activities.

items.html: Biopsy in suspected retinoblastoma. Biopsy is avoided because it risks seeding tumor cells, so diagnosis rests on examination and imaging.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: A 3-year-old has a retinal mass suspicious for retinoblastoma. Why is biopsy avoided?
src.explanation: so diagnosis rests on examination and imaging.

items.html: Eyelid hemangioma covering the visual axis. The priority is prompt referral to prevent amblyopia, because the obstruction has to be cleared while vision can still develop.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 33

src.question: A 2-year-old boy has an eyelid hemangioma covering the visual axis. What is the priority?
src.explanation: The obstruction has to be cleared while vision can still develop.

items.html: Complication of traumatic hyphema. Patients are monitored for rebleeding with a rise in intraocular pressure; the rebleed risk peaks in the first three to five days.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 25

src.question: A 17-year-old boy with a traumatic hyphema is being counseled. Which complication is he being monitored for over the next few days?
src.key: Rebleeding with a rise in intraocular pressure
src.explanation: Correct — the rebleed risk peaks in the first three to five days.

items.html: Punctate epithelial keratitis. It presents as a painful, photophobic red eye with reduced vision, with diffuse punctate fluorescein staining without an infiltrate, from exposure and surface drying.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 55

src.question: A 30-year-old woman has a painful, photophobic red right eye with reduced vision. Fluorescein shows diffuse punctate uptake across the cornea without a discrete infiltrate. She has been using a hairdryer at close range and has dry eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Diffuse punctate staining without an infiltrate, from exposure and surface drying.

items.html: Red flags in a red eye. Reduced vision and true pain move a red eye out of the benign category and separate a dangerous cause from a benign one.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 8

src.question: A patient presents with a red eye. Which two findings are the red flags that separate a dangerous cause from a benign one?
src.explanation: Correct — those two are what move a red eye out of the benign category.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Raised pigmented choroidal lesion. With orange pigment and associated subretinal fluid, the next step is urgent ophthalmology referral; orange pigment, thickness and subretinal fluid separate melanoma from a benign nevus.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 45

src.question: A 63-year-old man is found on routine examination to have a raised pigmented choroidal lesion with orange pigment and associated subretinal fluid. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Orange pigment, thickness and subretinal fluid are the features that separate melanoma from a benign nevus.

items.html: Lumbar puncture in idiopathic intracranial hypertension. With papilledema, the expected finding is a raised opening pressure with normal constituents.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 46

src.question: A 29-year-old woman with papilledema has a lumbar puncture. What finding is expected?
src.key: A raised opening pressure with normal constituents
src.explanation: Correct — that is the pattern in idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Relative afferent pupillary defect. Optic neuritis can explain it, because the defect lies in the afferent pathway, which is the optic nerve.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 26

src.question: A 41-year-old man is found to have a relative afferent pupillary defect. Which of the following would explain it?
src.explanation: Correct — a defect of the afferent pathway, which is the optic nerve.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Small flat uniformly pigmented choroidal lesion. With drusen on its surface and no subretinal fluid, management is photographic surveillance; flatness, drusen and absent fluid all favor a benign nevus.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 49

src.question: A 60-year-old man has a small, flat, uniformly pigmented choroidal lesion with drusen on its surface and no subretinal fluid. What is the most appropriate management?
src.explanation: Flatness, drusen and absent fluid all favor a benign nevus.

items.html: Stages of trachoma. Trachoma progresses through four stages: follicles, scarring, entropion and opacity.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 46

src.question: Through which four stages does trachoma progress?

items.html: Presentation of retinoblastoma. The two most common presenting features are leukocoria (a white pupil) and strabismus (a squint).
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 41

src.question: A 20-month-old boy has leukocoria and a convergent squint. Which two presenting features are most common in retinoblastoma?
src.explanation: Correct — a white pupil and a squint are the two classic presentations.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Branch retinal artery occlusion. It causes sudden painless loss of part of the visual field, with a pale wedge of retina in one artery's territory producing loss of the opposite field.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 41

src.question: A 66-year-old man has sudden painless loss of the lower half of his visual field in one eye. Fundoscopy shows a wedge of pale retina above the macula. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: A pale wedge in one artery's territory, producing loss of the opposite field.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Orbital and lid contusion. Lid bruising and swelling with normal vision, equal reactive pupils and full eye movements indicate soft tissue injury with normal ocular function.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 31

src.question: A 24-year-old man was struck in the eye two days ago. He has lid bruising and swelling but vision is 6/6, the pupils are equal and reactive, and eye movements are full. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Correct — soft tissue injury with normal ocular function.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Superior division oculomotor lesion. It causes ptosis and impaired elevation, because the superior division supplies levator palpebrae and superior rectus.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 39

src.question: A lesion affects only the superior division of the oculomotor nerve. Which deficits result?
src.explanation: The superior division supplies levator palpebrae and superior rectus.

items.section_title: 2.3 · The accommodation reflex, and light-near dissociation Objective e
items.html: Near response. On shifting gaze from distance to near, the lens thickens, the pupils constrict and the eyes converge; it acts on lens, pupil and globes together.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: A patient shifts gaze from a distant sign to a book. Which three changes make up this near response?
src.key: Lens thickens, pupils constrict, eyes converge
src.explanation: The near response acts on lens, pupil and globes together.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Acute Horner syndrome with neck pain after chiropractic manipulation. The next step is urgent vascular imaging, because carotid dissection must be identified before it embolizes.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 15

src.question: A 44-year-old woman has acute Horner syndrome with neck pain after a chiropractic manipulation. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Carotid dissection must be identified before it embolises.

items.html: Retinal detachment presentation. Flashes of light, a shower of floaters and a curtain moving across the vision of one eye, with myopia as the risk factor, suggest rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: A 58-year-old myope describes a shower of floaters, flashes of light, and a curtain moving across the vision of one eye. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Flashes, floaters and a curtain, with myopia as the risk factor.

items.html: Corneal foreign body. Photophobia, tearing and foreign body sensation with nothing on diffuse light call for slit lamp examination as the next step: larger objects show on diffuse light, smaller ones need the slit lamp.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: A 34-year-old machinist has photophobia, tearing and a foreign body sensation after a day at the lathe. Diffuse light shows nothing. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Larger objects show on diffuse light; smaller ones need the slit lamp.

items.html: Basilar skull fracture. After head trauma, raccoon eyes, Battle sign and hemotympanum together should raise suspicion of a basilar skull fracture; they are the indirect signs.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: Which combination of findings should raise a basilar skull fracture after head trauma?
src.key: Raccoon eyes, Battle sign and hemotympanum
src.explanation: Those are the indirect signs.

items.html: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis. Neonates are often treated in hospital because there is often concomitant pneumonia or pneumonitis; the lung involvement is what drives admission.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: Why are neonates with chlamydial conjunctivitis often treated in hospital?
src.key: Because there is often concomitant pneumonia or pneumonitis
src.explanation: Correct — the lung involvement is what drives admission.

items.html: Herpes simplex keratitis. A true dendrite, a branching corneal lesion on fluorescein with terminal end bulbs, is pathognomonic for herpes simplex, and the treatment is oral antiviral therapy for ten days.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 59

src.question: A 26-year-old man has a painful red eye with photophobia. Fluorescein under cobalt blue light shows a branching corneal lesion with small knobs at the ends of each branch (terminal end bulbs). Which is the most appropriate treatment?
src.key: Oral antiviral therapy for ten days
src.explanation: Correct — a true dendrite with terminal end bulbs is pathognomonic for herpes simplex.

items.html: Amaurosis fugax. The term for fleeting blindness, meaning monocular episodic visual loss.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 5

src.question: A 65-year-old woman describes fleeting blindness. Which term is this a synonym for?
src.explanation: monocular episodic visual loss.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Evaluating glaucoma. Tonometry and gonioscopy are the two tests: tonometry measures pressure, and gonioscopy views the angle.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: A 63-year-old woman is being evaluated for glaucoma. Which two tests are used?
src.explanation: Correct; tonometry measures pressure, gonioscopy views the angle.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Painful red eye with a hazy cornea. Intraocular pressure is measured first, by tonometry or gonioscopy; expect 40 to 80 mmHg.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: A 61-year-old woman has a painful red eye with a hazy cornea. Which measurement is made first?
src.explanation: by tonometry or gonioscopy; expect 40 to 80 mmHg.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Central retinal artery occlusion. Profound painless loss of vision in one eye over seconds that does not recover, with a pale retina.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 38

src.question: A 76-year-old man with carotid disease describes vision in one eye going dark instantly two hours ago and not returning. He has no pain. The retina is pale. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Correct; profound painless loss over seconds that does not recover.

items.html: Amaurosis fugax outlook. About 85% recover fully, and the remainder progress to a central retinal artery occlusion.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 8

src.question: A 67-year-old woman with amaurosis fugax asks what happens next. What is the usual outlook?
src.explanation: and the remainder progress to a central retinal artery occlusion.

items.section_title: 3.6 · The four retinal vascular occlusions Objective a5
items.html: Central retinal vein occlusion. Sudden painless loss of vision with the "blood and thunder" fundus: disc swelling, dilated, engorged veins, cotton wool spots and hemorrhages in every quadrant.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss current - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 34
12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 32

src.question: A 63-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. Fundoscopy shows a swollen disc, dilated veins, cotton wool spots and hemorrhages across all four quadrants. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: The blood and thunder fundus with disc swelling.

also.explanation: The 'blood and thunder' fundus — hemorrhages in every quadrant with engorged veins.

items.html: Posterior capsule opacification. Vision clouds again after cataract surgery because residual lens epithelial cells cloud the capsule.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 39

src.question: A 68-year-old woman's vision clouds again two years after cataract surgery. What has most likely happened?
src.explanation: Residual lens epithelial cells cloud the capsule.

items.section_title: 4.10 · Uveal melanoma, nevus and conjunctival melanoma
items.html: Iris freckles. Flat, multifocal, bilateral surface pigment on the irides, with no stromal involvement.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors - Dr Rappa.pptx, Slide 48

src.question: A 45-year-old man has flat, multifocal, bilateral surface pigment on both irides. What is this?
src.explanation: Surface pigment with no stromal involvement.

items.html: Xanthelasma. Soft yellow plaques lying in the eyelid skin near the inner corner, typically on both sides.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: Name the condition shown.
src.explanation: Soft yellow plaques lying in the eyelid skin near the inner corner, typically on both sides.

items.section_title: 5.6 · Lid lacerations, contusion and periorbital hematoma
items.html: Orbital contusion. Blunt injury fills the surface with hemorrhage and swells the lids, with no open wound.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 32

src.question: Name the condition shown.
src.explanation: Blunt injury has filled the surface with hemorrhage and swollen the lids, with no open wound.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Acute severe eye pain with halos, hazy cornea and fixed dilated pupil. With a shallow anterior chamber and ciliary injection, tonometry is the immediate next step: measuring the intraocular pressure confirms the diagnosis.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 13

src.question: A 48-year-old patient has acute blurring of vision and severe pain in the left eye that began 30 minutes ago, with halos around lights. They are nauseated and have vomited. The pain started while they were relaxing on their porch. Temperature 36.9°C, pulse 90/min, blood pressure 130/90 mm Hg, respirations 20/min. Examination reveals a shallow anterior chamber, a hazy cornea, a fixed moderately dilated pupil and ciliary injection. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
src.explanation: Measuring the intraocular pressure confirms the diagnosis and is the immediate step.

items.html: Episcleritis. It is self-limiting and often needs no specific treatment; management is reassurance, with lubricants for comfort.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 48

src.question: A 33-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of sectoral eye redness with mild irritation, each resolving within a week or two. Vision is always normal. What is the appropriate management?
src.explanation: Episcleritis is self-limiting and often needs no specific treatment.

items.html: Posterior vitreous detachment. Cataract surgery, myopia and ocular trauma all make it more likely.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 37

src.question: A 69-year-old woman has had cataract surgery. Which later complication is she now more likely to develop?
src.explanation: Correct — cataract surgery, myopia and ocular trauma all make it more likely.

items.html: Hyperopia. The eye is too short, and accommodative effort at near produces headaches and eye strain when reading, with normal distance vision.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 19

src.question: A 9-year-old boy has headaches and eye strain when reading, and his distance vision is normal. Which refractive error is most likely?
src.explanation: Correct — the eye is too short and accommodative effort at near produces the strain.

items.section_title: 3.8 · Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy Objective a6
items.html: Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Altitudinal field loss on waking, with normal inflammatory markers and no arteritic symptoms such as scalp tenderness or jaw claudication.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 52

src.question: A 59-year-old man with hypertension and sleep apnea wakes with painless loss of the lower half of the visual field in one eye. There is no scalp tenderness or jaw claudication, and the inflammatory markers are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Altitudinal field loss on waking, with normal inflammatory markers and no arteritic symptoms.

items.html: Urgent conjunctivitis. Contact lens wear, immunocompromise, recent surgery, a foreign body, corneal opacity or no improvement in 24 hours all make it urgent.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 41

src.question: A 34-year-old contact lens wearer has a red right eye with thick yellow discharge and lids stuck together on waking. There is no preauricular node. What makes this presentation urgent rather than routine?
src.explanation: Contact lens wear, immunocompromise, recent surgery, a foreign body, corneal opacity or no improvement in 24 hours all make it urgent.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Third nerve palsy. The eye is "down and out" because of unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique: the muscles the third nerve does not supply are the ones left working.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 39

src.question: Why is a third nerve palsy described as producing an eye that is 'down and out'?
src.key: Unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique
src.explanation: Correct — the muscles the third nerve does NOT supply are the ones left working.

items.html: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Classic picture: a woman with a raised body mass index, daily headaches, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, papilledema with bilateral disc swelling, and normal neuroimaging.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 4

src.question: A 24-year-old woman with a raised body mass index has daily headaches, pulsatile tinnitus and transient visual obscurations. Fundoscopy shows bilateral disc swelling. Neuroimaging is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Correct — the classic demographic, with papilledema and normal imaging.

items.html: Trachoma. Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis; it progresses through follicles, tarsal scarring, entropion with trichiasis, and corneal opacity.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 45

src.question: A 35-year-old woman who grew up in a region with poor sanitation has scarring of the tarsal conjunctiva with lashes turned inward and a corneal opacity. What organism is responsible?
src.explanation: Trachoma progresses through follicles, tarsal scarring, entropion with trichiasis, and corneal opacity.

items.html: Anterior uveitis. It involves the iris (iritis), or the iris and ciliary body (iridocyclitis).
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 62

src.question: Which structures does ANTERIOR uveitis involve?
src.key: The iris, or the iris and ciliary body
src.explanation: Correct — iritis, or iridocyclitis.

items.html: Fluorescein. Instilled and viewed under a blue light; it pools in epithelial defects and reveals abrasions, ulcers and foreign bodies.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 10

src.question: A 29-year-old woman has a suspected corneal abrasion. How is fluorescein used?
src.key: Instilled and viewed under a blue light
src.explanation: Correct — it pools in epithelial defects and reveals abrasions, ulcers and foreign bodies.

items.html: Globe rupture. A peaked, teardrop-shaped pupil points toward the rupture site, and the anterior chamber deepens with a posterior rupture.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma, Slide 17

src.question: A 44-year-old man was struck in the eye with a squash ball. Vision is hand movements only. Examination shows a peaked, teardrop-shaped pupil and a deep anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: A peaked pupil points toward the rupture site; the chamber deepens with a posterior rupture.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Glaucoma — acute closed-angle and chronic open-angle Objective a2
items.html: Acute angle-closure glaucoma. A shallow anterior chamber predisposes to it: a crowded angle is what allows closure when the pupil dilates.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 16

src.question: A 56-year-old woman has confirmed acute angle-closure glaucoma. Which anatomical feature predisposed her to it?
src.explanation: Correct — a crowded angle is what allows closure when the pupil dilates.

items.html: Bilateral retinoblastoma. It implies a heritable germline mutation, with implications for siblings and for second malignancies.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 42

src.question: A 2-year-old girl is diagnosed with bilateral retinoblastoma. What does bilateral disease imply?
src.explanation: Correct — bilateral disease is germline, with implications for siblings and for second malignancies.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Fourth cranial nerve. It supplies the superior oblique, which depresses the adducted eye, hence vertical diplopia worse on downgaze.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 43

src.question: Which statement correctly describes the muscle the fourth cranial nerve supplies and its action?
src.key: Superior oblique, which depresses the adducted eye
src.explanation: Correct — hence vertical diplopia worse on downgaze.

items.html: First-line treatment of open-angle glaucoma. A prostaglandin analog; prostaglandins or beta blockers lead, and cholinergic agents are third or fourth line.
cites: 12. Acute Vision Loss, Slide 19

src.question: A 58-year-old woman with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma is started on treatment. Which class is first line?
src.explanation: Prostaglandins or beta blockers lead; cholinergic agents are third or fourth line.

items.html: Orbital cellulitis. The usual source of infection is the paranasal sinuses, which is why imaging covers the sinuses as well as the orbits.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 52

src.question: A 12-year-old boy has orbital cellulitis. What is the usual source of the infection?
src.explanation: Correct — which is why imaging covers the sinuses as well as the orbits.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Argyll Robertson pupil. Small, irregular pupils in both eyes that do not react to light but constrict briskly on near effort: light-near dissociation, "accommodates but does not react".
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology, Slide 31

src.question: A 52-year-old man has small, irregular pupils bilaterally. They do NOT react to light, but constrict briskly on near effort. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Correct — light-near dissociation with small irregular pupils; 'accommodates but does not react'.

items.html: Hyperopia and ocular emergencies. Hyperopic patients are warned about acute angle-closure glaucoma, because the short eye has a crowded anterior segment.
cites: Chronic Vision Loss & Tumors, Slide 19

src.question: A 58-year-old hyperopic woman is warned about one particular ocular emergency. Which is it?
src.explanation: Correct — the short eye has a crowded anterior segment.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Peripheral fourth nerve lesion. A peripheral lesion after the nerve exits gives an ipsilateral deficit, in the same side eye.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: A 37-year-old woman has a peripheral fourth nerve lesion. Which eye is affected relative to the lesion?
src.explanation: a peripheral lesion after the nerve exits gives an ipsilateral deficit.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies Objective f5
items.html: Acquired fourth nerve palsy. The likely causes are trauma and microvascular disease, with even mild trauma sufficient.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: A 46-year-old man has an acquired fourth nerve palsy. What are the likely causes?
src.explanation: with even mild trauma sufficient.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Marcus Gunn pupil. The lesion is pre-chiasmal, in the retina or optic nerve.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: A 30-year-old woman has a Marcus Gunn pupil. Is the lesion pre- or post-chiasmal?
src.explanation: retina or optic nerve.

items.html: Ptosis of third nerve palsy versus Horner syndrome. Levator function distinguishes them: it is reduced in third nerve palsy and normal in Horner syndrome.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 49

src.question: Which feature distinguishes ptosis from a third nerve palsy from ptosis of Horner syndrome?
src.explanation: It is reduced in third nerve palsy and normal in Horner syndrome.

items.html: Upbeat nystagmus. New upbeat nystagmus is classified as concerning and non-physiologic, and it warrants work-up in adults.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 5

src.question: A 40-year-old man has new upbeat nystagmus. How is this finding classified?
src.explanation: and it warrants work-up in adults.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Relative afferent pupillary defect. Detected with the swinging flashlight test: moving the light to the affected eye makes both pupils dilate.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: A 26-year-old man has reduced vision in one eye. Which bedside maneuver detects a relative afferent pupillary defect?
src.explanation: Moving the light to the affected eye makes both pupils dilate.

items.section_title: 2.4 · Anisocoria — deciding which pupil is abnormal Objective f7
items.html: Physiologic anisocoria. Mild anisocoria, equal in light and dark, with normal lids and movements, needs only reassurance and no work-up.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: A 43-year-old man has 0.3 mm of anisocoria, equal in light and dark, with normal lids and movements. What is the most appropriate step?
src.explanation: This is physiologic anisocoria and needs no work-up.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The four named pupils Objectives f1–f4
items.html: Argyll Robertson pupils. Look for the associated finding of sensory ataxia, from tabes dorsalis with posterior column involvement.
cites: 11. Neuro-Ophthalmology STUDENT VERSION 2026.pptx, Slide 32

src.question: A 55-year-old man with Argyll Robertson pupils asks what else to look for. Which associated finding should be sought?
src.explanation: from tabes dorsalis with posterior column involvement.

items.html: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. The most common type of retinal detachment: full-thickness retinal breaks let liquefied vitreous behind the retina.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 35

src.question: Which type of retinal detachment is the most common?
src.explanation: Full-thickness retinal breaks let liquefied vitreous behind the retina.

items.html: Mechanism in ocular trauma. Whether the injury was blunt or sharp, and high or low velocity, most changes the level of concern, because it predicts the injury pattern.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 8

src.question: Which detail about the mechanism most changes the level of concern in ocular trauma?
src.key: Blunt or sharp, high or low velocity
src.explanation: That is what predicts the injury pattern.

items.html: Basilar skull fracture. Suggested by raccoon eyes (bruising around both eyes), Battle sign (bruising behind the ear) and hemotympanum (blood behind the eardrum) together.
cites: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: A 39-year-old fell from a ladder. She has bruising around both eyes, bruising behind one ear, and blood behind the eardrum. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Raccoon eyes, Battle sign and hemotympanum together.

items.html: Entropion. It produces foreign body sensation because the inward-turned lashes rub the globe.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 12

src.question: Which symptom does entropion produce?
src.explanation: Correct — the inward-turned lashes rub the globe.

items.html: Dermatochalasis. Treated with blepharoplasty, the surgical removal of the excess skin.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 15

src.question: What is the treatment for dermatochalasis?
src.explanation: Correct — surgical removal of the excess skin.

items.html: Chalazion. A firm, painless, non-tender, slowly enlarging eyelid nodule is managed conservatively first, with warm compresses with gentle massage.
cites: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: A 35-year-old woman has a firm, painless lump in her upper eyelid that has been slowly enlarging for three weeks. It is not tender. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
src.explanation: Correct — the painless, slowly enlarging nodule is a chalazion, managed conservatively first.
